REVIEWOpen Access Page 2 of 40

inception of QDs research [1]. QDs is quasi-zero-dimensional semiconductor nanocrys-
tals consisting  of a small  number of atoms that bind excitons in H-dimensional space, 
with a radius generally smaller than or close to the exciton bolometric radius, between 
1  and  10  nm.  The  electronic  structure  exhibits  a  unique  set  of  optoelectronic  proper-
ties due to the change from a continuous energy level structure to a quasi-split energy 
level, i.e., with quantum-limited effects [2–4]. As (1) QDs can be tuned in size or struc-
tural  composition,  leading  to  spectral  emission  in  the  entire  visible  region  [5–6].  (2) 
with a broad excitation spectrum and narrow emission spectrum, and its full width at 
half  maximum  (FWHM)  is  narrow  [7–8].  (3)  Excellent  photostability  [9–11].  (4)  Long 
fluorescence lifetime, surface chemical plasticity, and good biocompatibility [12–13]. In 
addition,  semiconductor  colloidal  QDs  also  have  excellent  properties  such  as  solution 
processability and high color purity [14].

Currently,  researchers  have  established  a  variety  of  mechanisms  for  QDs  synthesis, 
which are divided into two main categories, namely physical preparation methods and 
chemical  preparation  methods  [15–19].  The  most  common  is  chemical  preparation, 
which is divided into two main methods: one is organic synthesis, and the other is syn-
thesis in the aqueous phase [20–22]. Organic synthesis of QDs employs organometallic 
precursors (e.g., Cd(CH3)2, Zn(CH3)2), which are highly unstable, sensitive to water and 
oxygen, toxic, flammable, and explosive, and the preparation process can only be carried 
out in a glove box filled with nitrogen. The process is complex and not suitable for large-
scale production. Comparatively, the aqueous-phase synthesis is simple to operate and 
have  a  low  cost.  It  requires  no  further  modification,  and  QDs  such  as  CdS,  CdSe,  and 
ZnSe have been successfully obtained in aqueous solution [23–26]. QDs has a high spe-
cific surface area with undercoordinated surface atoms, leading to pronounced surface 
defects  that  facilitate  atomic  aggregation  and  agglomeration,  resulting  in  poor  optical 
properties  of  QDs  [27].  Over  the  years,  researchers  have  made  many  efforts  to  elimi-
nate the surface defects of QDs, the most common of which is to modify the surface of 
QDs  using  various  organic  and  inorganic  materials. The  surface  modification  of  semi-
conductor fluorescent QDs mainly includes inorganic shell layer passivation surface and 
functionalized group modification surface. For instance, Hines and Guyot-Sionnes first 
proposed to wrap 1–2 monolayers of ZnS shell layers on top of CdSe nanocrystals with a 
particle size of 3 nm, and eventually the quantum yield (QY) of QDs based on the CdSe/
ZnS core-shell structure was enhanced to 50% [28]. Murcia et al. used acoustic chemis-
try driven synthesis of CdSe QDs and subsequently coated ZnS on the surface of CdSe 
QDs  also  by  acoustic  chemistry  driven,  with  a  QY  of  50%-60%  and  FWHM  of  25  nm 
[29]. Roy et al. reported a microwave-assisted synthesis of water-soluble CdSe/ZnS QDs 
with a maximum emission wavelength of 511 nm to 596 nm [30]. Functionalized groups 
modifying the surface of QDs commonly include organic small molecule modifications 
and organic polymer modifications, as Qian et al. combined experimental and theoreti-
cal approaches to systematically investigate the surface chemistry of a series of graphene 
QDs functionalized with small organic molecules. The surface functionalization of gra-
phene QDs with alcohols, amines and thiols can effectively modulate the fluorescence of 
graphene QDs, and demonstrate that amines can significantly improve the QY of modi-
fied graphene QDs [31].

As  shown  in  Figs.  1  and  2,  heavy  metals  in  Cd-based  QDs  may  be  relatively  harm-
ful  to  the  environment  and  living  organisms,  and  in  severe  cases  can  lead  to  serious 

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  Page 3 of 40

Fig. 1  Environmental impact of QDs pollution from informal disposal activities

Fig. 2  Toxicity mechanism of QDs to human beings

chronic  diseases  and  cancers  [32–33].  The  UN  Global  E-waste  Monitor  2024  reports 
that global electronic waste (e-waste) has surged to 62 million metric tons, with heavy 
metal emissions from this sector contributing 15–20% of the total industrial discharge. 
In response, multilateral environmental conventions have established a targeted gover-
nance framework, integrating legally binding protocols for toxic substance phase-outs. 
The Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment (1972) establishes foundational 
environmental rights and obligations under Principle 1: “Humankind bears the solemn 
duty to preserve intergenerational ecological integrity, entitling all to a healthy environ-
ment while mandating stewardship for future generations.” Principle 21 further codifies 
state  responsibility  to  “prevent  transboundary  environmental  harm  through  toxic  sub-
stance  control.”  In  accordance  with  this  framework,  the  Rio  Declaration  on  Environ-
ment and Development (1992) articulates the “Precautionary Principle” in Principle 15: 
“Where  threats  of  serious  or  irreversible  damage  exist,  scientific  uncertainty  shall  not 
postpone cost-effective preventive measures, requiring states to implement anticipatory 
pollution controls through risk-weighted regulatory action and technology-forcing stan-
dards.”  The  Precautionary  Principle  prioritizes  early  intervention  through  legal  norms 

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  
 
 Page 4 of 40

enacted by public authorities to mitigate potential harm at its source. The jurispruden-
tial  essence  of  the  precautionary  principle  is  enshrined  in  the  Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 
Project judgment (1997) by the International Court of Justice (ICJ):“Vigilance and pre-
vention are non-derogable obligations in environmental governance, as ecological harm 
is  characterized  by  irreversibility  and  remediation  inherently  constrained  by  scientific 
and  technical  limitations. This  ruling underscores the imperative for anticipatory legal 
interventions, even amid epistemic uncertainty, to avert systemic risks posed by persis-
tent pollutants.1 For QDs not to cause harmful results in terms of environmental pollu-
tion, legal norms must actively take measures to prevent such damage and must ensure 
that these measures are effectively implemented, which is an environmental compliance 
obligation. The development of eco-friendly QD synthesis technologies aligns with green 
chemistry principles and fulfills the environmental compliance requirements of the pre-
cautionary principle.

To date, eco-friendly QDs such as Indium Phosphide (InP) [34–35], graphene [36–37], 
CuInS2 [38–39], Zn-based, etc., have also been developed to a large extent. For instance, 
InP  QDs  has  superior  features  such  as  a  larger  exciton  wave  radius  and  high  carrier 
mobility,  stronger  quantum  confinement  effect,  wide  spectral  tunability,  and  larger 
intrinsic absorption coefficient, making them one of the excellent alternative materials 
for Cd-based QDs [40–41]. Yet, InP QDs also suffer from poor electron-binding ability, 
weak performance stability, and low QY. Graphene QDs, a new star in the family of car-
bon-based fluorescent nanomaterials, have received extensive attention from research-
ers  globally  in  recent  years  [42].  Graphene  QDs  possess  high  chemical  stability,  upper 
fluorescence  QY,  strong  resistance  to  photobleaching,  lower  cytotoxicity,  and  good 
biocompatibility.  In  addition,  they  also  have  significant  photoluminescence  properties, 
and fluorescence spectra with different emission wavelengths from the deep UV region 
to the IR region band can be obtained by changing the raw material ratios or synthesis 
pathways [43–44]. However, graphene QDs also often have broad emission peaks due to 
defective luminescence as well as poor carrier injection and low luminescence efficiency, 
limiting their more profound development in the field of illumination [45–47].

This paper first provides a comprehensive review of global regulatory frameworks gov-
erning heavy metal contaminants, particularly Cd, Hg, and Pb, with a focus on environ-
mental  compliance  requirements  in  key  jurisdictions,  including  the  United  States,  the 
European Union, China, and Japan. The examination encompassed five critical dimen-
sions: hazardous waste management protocols, production/usage restrictions, emission 
control  standards,  occupational  safety  regulations,  and  public  right-to-know  obliga-
tions. These legislative initiatives aim to mitigate heavy metal pollution through source 
control  and  exposure  minimization,  thereby  directly  driving  the  advancement  of  eco-
friendly quantum dot alternatives. Building on global regulatory frameworks, this study 
analyzes three eco-friendly QDs—InP QDs, graphene QDs, and ternary CuInS2 QDs by 
comparing  their  synthesis  methods  (hot  injection,  solvothermal,  and  thermal  decom-
position) and applications in optoelectronics, biomedicine, and environmental sensing. 
The  analysis  highlighted  critical  challenges:  QY  limitations  (> 35%  energy  loss),  ambi-
ent stability issues, and scalability constraints (± 15% batch variability). To address these 
issues,  we  propose  machine-learning-optimized  synthesis,  atomic-layer  encapsulation, 

1  Gabětkovo-Nagymaros Project, supra footnote 11, para. 14.

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  Page 5 of 40

and  microfluidic  production,  ultimately  envisioning  hybrid  architectures  via  plasma-
enhanced doping to achieve > 95% quantum efficiency.

2  International and National regulatory frameworks governing heavy metal 
containment in QDs
2.1  International convention

The elimination of Cd, Pd, Hg, and their toxic and hazardous compounds at the sources 
of  production,  storage,  trade,  and  transfer  has  been  universally  recognized  in  the  for-
mulation  of  many  international  conventions.  An  international  convention  is  a  writ-
ten agreement between subjects of international law on mutual rights and obligations, 
which reflects the common will and interests of state parties [48]. As the development 
of  international  environmental  issues  will  ultimately  affect  the  alteration  of  the  entire 
Earth’s  ecosystem,  their  outcome  is  closely  linked  to  the  survival  of  human  beings  on 
Earth. In addition, emerging international environmental problems, such as holes in the 
ozone layer and transboundary waste transfer, cannot be solved by a single country and 
need to be regulated by multilateral international conventions of a global and regional 
nature  [49].  As  delineated  in  Fig.  3,  five  pivotal  conventions  (Basel,  Rotterdam,  Stock-
holm, Bamako, and Minamata) form the BRS + governance architecture. These regimes 
aim to collectively address the global challenges of heavy metal management by harmo-
nizing standards to control the transboundary movement of hazardous substances and 
their impacts on human health and the environment.

Non-compliant  states  primarily  risk  reputational  damage  or  trade  privilege  revoca-
tion  rather  than  coercive  penalties,  as  evidenced  by  persistent  non-compliance  with 
the  Stockholm  Convention  mandates  on  toxic  substance  phase-outs,  where  Cd-based 
QDs  remain  prevalent  because  of  economic  prioritization  and  technological  path 
dependencies. For example, the Minamata Convention’s decade-long adoption timeline 

Fig. 3  The BRS + governance architectures on the limitation of heavy metal

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  
 Page 6 of 40

exemplifies how conflicting national interests (e.g., differentiated emission responsibili-
ties between industrialized and developing economies) protract multilateral consensus 
building.

2.2  2.2 National legislation

National legislation on heavy metal contaminants (Cd, Hg, Pb) emphasizes source con-
trol  through  production  bans  and  import  restrictions.  As  delineated  in  Table  1,  the 
United States implements prior informed consent (PIC) protocols, mandating dual obli-
gations:  exporter  disclosure  of  chemical  profiles  for  specified  imports  and  consumer 
notification requirements for toxic substance-containing products. In contrast, the EU 
adopts preventative measures by limiting heavy metal concentrations in electronics and 
batteries while incentivizing safer alternatives through Horizon Europe funding mecha-
nisms. Major economies, including China, Japan, and South Korea, operationalize three-
phase regulatory models: (i) formal classification of Cd/Pb/Hg compounds as hazardous 
substances,  (ii)  manufacturing  prohibitions  coupled  with  product  toxicity  thresholds, 
and  (iii)  import  control  regimes  targeting  non-compliant  goods.  These  frameworks 
demonstrate  regulatory  convergence  in  life-cycle  management  of  toxic  metals  despite 
jurisdictional variations in implementation timelines.

Consequently,  this  regulatory  landscape  has  catalyzed  substantial  innovations  across 
multiple  domains,  including  the  development  of  toxic  metal  alternatives,  optimization 
of synthesis processes, and implementation of comprehensive risk mitigation strategies. 
This transformative shift represents a convergence of regulatory alignment and sustain-
able material science innovation, marking a new era in nanomaterial development and 
application [50].

3  Eco-friendly QDs from an environmental compliance perspective

With  the  enhancement  of  environmental  awareness  and  the  increasing  strictness  of 
environmental  regulations,  various  industries  are  undergoing  a  transformation  toward 
sustainable  development. The  development  of  eco-friendly  QDs  aligns  with  this  trend, 
contributing to the sustainable development of quantum dot-related industries. By meet-
ing market demands for the optical properties of quantum dot materials while reducing 
environmental  impacts,  it  achieves  a  harmonious  integration  of  economic  growth  and 
environmental  protection.  The  advancement  of  eco-friendly  QDs  can  drive  the  entire 
quantum dot industry to transition toward green and environmentally friendly practices, 
prompting  relevant  enterprises  to  research,  develop,  and  adopt  more  sustainable  pro-
duction processes and materials. This encourages collaborative efforts across the entire 
industrial  chain  to  improve  resource  utilization  efficiency,  reduce  pollutant  emissions, 
and  enhance  the  overall  environmental  performance  of  the  industry,  thereby  better 
addressing the challenges posed by increasingly stringent environmental regulations and 
market  demands  for  eco-friendly  products.Therefore,  this  section  mainly  summarizes 
the  different  environmentally  friendly  QDs  synthesis  methods  and  the  corresponding 
environmental protection requirements for the development of QDs in modern society.

3.1  InP QDs

Recently, InP-based QDs has become one of the hot alternatives to Cd-based QDs due

3.1.1  Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs

The  solvothermal  method  represents  an  efficient  and  rapid  approach  for  synthesizing 
highly  crystalline  and  monodisperse  InP  QDs.  This  synthetic  route  involves  the  intro-
duction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under 
an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers 
into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling 
effective  bandgap  engineering.  However,  the  method  requires  high  temperature  and 
Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explo-
sion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause 
a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal 
synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stabil-
ity.  These  QDs  exhibited  small  particle  sizes,  tunable  within  the  range  of  2.5–3.7  nm, 
achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temper-
ature  modulation  resulted  in  a  bandgap  tuning  range  of  approximately  0.4  eV  within 
the  visible  spectrum.  The  established  methodology  for  InP  QDs  synthesis  serves  as  a 
valuable  reference  for  fabricating  other  III-V  semiconductor  QDs.  Nozik  et  al.  further 
employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size 
of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [51]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvo-
thermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a 
remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor 
offers  significant  advantages  over  P(TMS)₃,  being  both  less  toxic  and  more  cost-effec-
tive, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis 
[52]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-
friendly,  and  low-cost  precursors  to  synthesize  InP/ZnS  core-shell  QDs  with  tunable 
fluorescence  properties  through  the  green  solvothermal  method,  achieving  an  impres-
sive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [53].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the 
controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis condi-
tions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to 
industrialization.  In  the  future,  synergistic  breakthroughs  in  performance  and  sustain-
ability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation 
and green process iteration.

3.1.2  Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs

The heating method is a reliable and scalable technique for colloidal nanocrystal synthe-
sis, which enables controlled nucleation and crystal growth by dissolving precursors and 
ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, sta-
bilizers and heating rate, high quality nanocrystals comparable to thermal injection can 
be produced. However, the decomposition of ligands (e.g., oleylamine) at high tempera-
tures releases amine gases that irritate the respiratory tract. These gases participate in 
photochemical reactions to form secondary pollutants such as ozone. Rapid nucleation 
is also prone to causing lattice distortion and high defect densities in QDs. To mitigate 
environmental impact, solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine) can be recovered via dis-
tillation or adsorption techniques, enabling closed-loop production. Figure 4a illustrates 
the fundamental process of nanocrystal formation in heated synthesis and its correlation 
with the reaction vessel temperature [54]. Pidluzhna et al. employed the heating method 
to  prepare  core-shell  InP/ZnS  hybrid  QDs,  as  depicted  in  Fig.  4b  Their  study  focused

controlled the emission wavelength of the InP core and optimized the thickness of the 
ZnS layer, thereby enhancing the quality of the QDs [56]. Kim et al. reported a simple 
one-pot heating method for synthesizing InP and InP/ZnS core-shell QDs. By precisely 
controlling the flow rate and crystal growth temperature, they successfully synthesized

poor process scalability are generally present. In the future, further breakthroughs can 
be achieved by developing bio-based ligands to replace oleylamine and coupling distilla-

post-processing passivation to reduce the defect density, as well as combining microflu-

3.1.3  Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs

The  hot-injection  method  achieves  the  separation  of  nucleation  and  growth  phases  by 
dissolving  the  precursor  in  organic  solvents  (e.g.,  octadecene,  oleylamine,  and  trioc-
tylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific tem-
perature  to  trigger  the  transient  supersaturation  of  the  solution,  which  allows  for  the 
homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both 
monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and 
active  agents  further  expand  the  product  system  [34–58].  However,  the  volatilization/
decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic com-
pounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and 
requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jam-
shidi  Zavaraki  et  al.  employed  a  hot  injection  method  to  synthesize  colloidal  InP  and 
ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers 
in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [59]. However, the stability of colloidal

3.2  Graphene QDs

As  an  emerging  eco-friendly  nanomaterial,  GQDs,  with  their  unique  physicochemical 
properties,  such  as  high  specific  surface  area  (300–600  m2/g),  excellent  optical  prop-
erties,  such  as  strong  fluorescence  properties,  tunable  fluorescence,  and  high  optical 
absorption  from  UV  to  IR  (  [70].  And  superior  electrical  properties,  such  as  high  car-
rier  mobility  with  a  mobility  of  more  than  15000  cm²  V− 1  S− 1  [71],  tunable  energy  gap 
(2  eV  − 0.02  eV)  (  [72].  And  favorable  biocompatibility,  enable  them  to  play  an  impor-
tant role in the fields of efficient water treatment and pollution control, air purification 
and greenhouse gas control, clean energy development and energy storage, eco-friendly 
materials  and  biodegradable  technology,  environmental  monitoring  and  sensor,  etc.  (( 
[73–74]).  GQDs  not  only  possess  a  series  of  excellent  properties  of  graphene,  but  also 
combine the small size and quantum-limited domain effect of QDs at the same time. The 
height range of GQDs is usually between 0.4 and 4 nm, and the thickness is 2–4 nm, i.e., 
between  2-layer  and  4-layer  graphene  sheets.  The  lateral  dimensions  are  typically  less 
than 100 nm, with most studies focusing on the range of less than 10 nm. The number of 
graphene layers usually consists of 1–10 layers of graphene, with most not exceeding 5 
layers (( [75–76]). Therefore, the efficient preparation of GQDs is of great significance to

3.2.1  Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs

The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene 
arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth 
direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient 
controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface 
defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the 
high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit 
their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified techno-
logical  paths  in  the  synthesis  of  GQDs,  such  as  Samra  et  al.  used  coke  as  a  raw  mate-
rial (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process 
(Fig.  9a),  and  spectroscopic  characterization  verified  the  feasibility  [77].  Xie  et  al.  syn-
thesized  highly  crystalline  monodispersed  bluish  N-GQDs  by  nitrogen-containing  3D 
nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig. 9b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping 
of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [78]. Zhou’s team innovated 
acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ 
filtration  to  obtain  water-soluble  blue-green  photoresponsive  N-GQDs  (1.5–3.7  nm, 
Fig.  10a),  circumventing  the  tedious  isolation  step  [79].  Tadyszak  et  al.  demonstrated 
that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the 
C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 
280–380 nm excitation (Fig. 10b) [80]. Soriano et al. developed GQDs fluorescence for 
the  detection  of  carbamates  in  water  by  using  mixed-acid  oxidation  to  modulate  the 
reaction time (Fig. 10c) [81].However, there are core limitations of this method, such as 
the strong corrosive waste liquid generated by the acid treatment method, the still low 
QY (< 20%) and the unclear mechanism of magnetic/optical property regulation. In the 
future, it could be attempted to develop green stripping technologies like laser/plasma to 
replace the strong acid process, construct doping-fluorescence-magnetism constitutive 
relationship models, and explore biomass carbon sources to reduce costs and increase 
efficiency.

3.3  CuInS2 QDs

CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-con-
taining QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low 
toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS 
directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable 
emission  ranging  from  500  to  800  nm  and  QY  up  to  80%),  exceptional  photostability 
and chemical robustness (manifested in superior photobleaching resistance and stabil-
ity under oxidative/acid-base environments), as well as cost-effectiveness and abundant 
elemental availability [86–88]. These distinctive characteristics render them a promising 
candidate  for  diverse  applications  spanning  biomedical  engineering,  renewable  energy 
technologies, and advanced display systems. However, the development of ternary CIS 
QDs  still  faces  several  challenges,  including  low  charge  injection  efficiency,  exciton 
quenching induced by interfacial space charge accumulation between charge transport 
layers, and interlayer miscibility during spin-coating processes [87–89]. Recent advance-
ments  in  core-shell  engineering  and  surface  chemistry  hold  promise  for  overcoming 
these  performance  limitations,  thereby  accelerating  the  practical  implementation  of 
green  nanotechnology.  The  following  sections  comprehensively  review  several  simple 
yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs.

In the study of the synthesis of CIS QDs, hot injection is an effective means of preparing 
high-quality  monodisperse  QDs,  but  is  limited  by  the  scarcity  of  low-toxicity  or  non-
toxic precursors. Zhu et al. applied a low-temperature hot injection preparation method 
to synthesize super-efficient green luminescent CIS QDs (the synthesis process appeared 
in Fig. 12). The introduction of S- Oil Amine (OAm)(S powder dissolved in ethylamine)

4  Eco-friendly QDs in different fields from an environmental compliance 
perspective

From  the  perspective  of  environmental  compliance,  eco-friendly  QDs  exhibit  signifi-
cant advantages in different applications. In the display and lighting fields, they do not 
contain heavy metals such as Pb, Cd, etc., which are subject to regulatory restrictions, 
and  fulfill  the  requirements  of  the  EU  RoHS  and  REACH  regulations  on  the  limits  of 
hazardous  substances  in  electronic  devices,  avoiding  the  risk  of  soil/water  contamina-
tion caused by the leakage of heavy metals in traditional Cd-based QDs, and at the same 
time reducing volatile organic emissions in the production process through the solution 
method  printing  process.  In  the  field  of  sensing,  low-toxicity  materials  represented  by 
GQDs  comply  with  the  International  Organization  for  Standardization  (ISO)  speci-
fication  on  the  biocompatibility  of  nanomaterials,  and  its  near-infrared  luminescent 
properties can reduce the use of chemical stains in in vivo imaging and circumvent the 
bioaccumulative toxicity of traditional fluorescent dyes. In the field of energy and envi-
ronment,  heavy  metal-free  QDs  can  be  used  in  solar  cells  through  a  simple  recycling 
process, complying with the requirements of the EU’s New Battery Law on the recycling 
rate  of  battery  components,  and  its  photocatalytic  degradation  of  pollutants  does  not 
produce secondary heavy metal pollution, conforming to the environmental protection 
standards of China’s Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution for 
the treatment of industrial wastewater.

4.1.2  InP QDs for quantum-dot light-emitting diode (QLEDs) applications

Driven by global policy initiatives—including China’s 14th Five-Year Plan strategic sup-

4.2  Applications of GQDs in different fields

4.2.1  GQD for solar cell applications

Graphene,  leveraging  its  exceptional  optoelectronic  properties,  biological  safety,  and 
processability advantages, has emerged as a research hotspot in the nanomaterials field. 
It  demonstrates  irreplaceable  application  value  across  disciplines  such  as  biomedicine, 
optoelectronic sensing, photovoltaic energy, and environmental science [120–121]. Over 
the  years,  continuous  exploration  of  graphene-based  materials  has  revealed  significant 
potential for enhancing solar cell performance through graphene-derived nanocrystals 
[122–123]. GQDs has achieved triple breakthroughs in photovoltaics: First, Ding’s team 
enhanced  cathode  interlayer  performance  in  polymer  solar  cells  via  edge-tetramethyl-
ammonium  functionalization  (GQD-TMA),  achieving  PCEs  of  7.01%  for  PCDTBT: 
PC₇₁BM and 8.80% for PTB7-Th: PC₇₁BM systems—significantly outperforming conven-
tional Ca/LiF/ZnO interlayers (< 6.5%) (compare J-V plots as displayed in Fig. 21). Sec-
ond, Wang introduced GQDs into molybdenum disulfide/indium phosphide (MoS₂/InP) 
van der Waals heterostructures, where photo-induced doping modulated the potential 
barrier height, boosting device PCE from 2.1 to 4.1%. Finally, Lin employed pulsed laser

GQDs-based  QLEDs  combine  the  unique  advantages  of  graphene  with  quantum  dot

GQDs  has  significant  advantages  in  sensor  applications:  its  excellent  optical  proper-

sensing  such  as  cell  imaging  and  in  vivo  detection.  In  addition,  their  relatively  simple

4.3  Applications of CIS QDs in different fields

4.3.1  CIS QDs for solar cells applications

CIS-based QDs offer significant advantages in solar cells: their 1.5–1.8 eV energy band 
structure matches the solar spectrum for efficient capture of visible-near-infrared light. 
Excellent carrier transport properties promote rapid photogenerated charge separation, 
enhancing short-circuit current and fill factor. Environmental friendliness (heavy metal 
free)  and  low-cost  solution  method  preparation  (spin  coating/inkjet  printing)  support 
scale-up production. Fine tuning of size, composition, and surface ligands optimizes the 
energy level matching of optoelectronic devices, simultaneously enhancing performance 
and long-term operational reliability [139–140].

As a representative study, Several teams have enhanced the performance of CIS QDs 
solar cells through interface engineering. For example, Konstantatos et al. used formic 
acid ligand exchange to construct a non-annealed CIS photoconductive film in a TiO2 
porous  network,  and  optimized  the  thickness  of  the  absorber  layer  and  carrier  mobil-
ity  to  improve  the  PCE  by  a  7.7-fold  factor,  from  0.05–1.16%.The  performance  evolu-
tion  was  quantitatively  verified  through  J-V  characterization,  with  the  corresponding 
curves  and  detailed  photovoltaic  parameters  documented  in  Fig.  25  [141]。Gao  et  al. 
design  TiO2-CIS  nanorod  arrays  to  achieve  the  highest  efficiency  of  11.7%  by  utilizing 
CIS  to  enhance  the  light  trapping  and  electron  injection  capabilities  [142].  Peng  et  al. 
modulated  the  TiO2/CIS  photoelectrode  interfacial  contact  by  heat  treatment  (300℃ 
optimum) to promote charge separation and transfer, and PCE was improved from 4.04 
to 4.68%. The photoelectric properties are characterized as shown in Fig. 26 [143].Wang 
et  al.  prepared  solar  cells  based  on  CIS  QDs  using  anatase  TiO2  nanodendrite  arrays 
instead of nanowires, and the results showed that the CIS QDSCs were able to achieve

4.3.2  CIS QDs for QLEDs applications

CIS  QDs  has  excellent  luminescence  performance  with  narrow  half-peak  width  (high 
color purity), adjustable light-emitting wavelengths (covering the visible range) and good 
QY, which enable high saturation and high contrast color displays, and their absorption 
and fluorescence spectra can be adjusted up to near-infrared wavelength bands. Com-
pared  to  conventional  cadmium-containing  QDs,  they  are  more  structurally  stable  in 
air and light conditions, contributing to the long-term operating life of QLEDs devices. 
The  HOMO/LUMO  energy  levels  can  be  optimized  by  adjusting  the  size  of  the  QDs, 
surface ligands, or alloying treatment, so as to achieve better interfacial matching with 
the  electron  and  hole  transport  layers  in  the  device,  and  to  improve  the  carrier  injec-
tion efficiency and luminescence efficiency [145–146]. For example, Li et al. used CIS/
ZnS  QDs  combined  with  blue  GaN  light-emitting  diode  chips  to  prepare  highly  effi-
cient  white  QLEDs  with  high  color  rendering  index  (CRI,  90)  and  4360  K  correlated 
color  temperature  [147].  Park  et  al.  introduced  CIS/ZnS/ZnS  QDs  and  showed  that

through  materials  engineering,  break  through  the  efficiency  bottleneck  by  combining 
with the innovation of device structure, and reduce the preparation cost through process 
optimization.  It  is  expected  that  CIS  QDs  will  be  applied  on  a  large  scale  in  the  fields 
of high-color gamut displays, bio-imaging, and optical communications, and especially 
have potential in the near-infrared optoelectronic devices and environmentally friendly 
display technologies.

4.3.3  CIS QDs for sensing applications

Due  to  its  unique  physicochemical  properties,  CuInS2  QDs  exhibit  significant  applica-
tion potential  in  pressure sensing, biosensing and optical sensing. In pressure sensing, 
its  quantum-limited-domain  effect  confers  size-sensitive  optical  properties,  and  exter-
nal  pressure-induced  lattice  aberrations  can  be  precisely  monitored  by  fluorescence 
wavelength  or  intensity  changes.In  the  field  of  biosensing,  the  near-infrared  lumines-
cence  characteristics  of  the  QDs  make  them  strongly  penetrating  to  biological  tissues, 
while the advantages of poor self-absorption and minimal background noise can signifi-
cantly enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of in vivo imaging, which is especially suitable 
for the non-invasive detection of biomarkers in deep tissues. In optical sensing, multi-
parameter  response  optical  sensing  arrays  can  be  constructed  to  realize  super-selec-
tive  identification  of  environmental  pollutants  or  gas  molecules  through  fluorescence 
resonance energy transfer or surface plasmon resonance mechanisms [150–151]. Safari 
et al. reported a fluorescence method for the detection of aspartic acid (Asp) in aque-
ous  media,  which  was  validated  based  on  CIS@ZnS  QDs  photoluminescent  sensors.It 
was found that the fluorescence intensity of CIS@ZnS QDs was significantly quenched 
by  the  addition  of  Asp  to  aqueous  media,  and  that  there  was  a  selective  fluorescence 
quenching response to Asp in the concentration range from 8.3 × 10− 7 M to 3.3 × 10− 4 M, 
with a limit of detection of 7.8 × 10− 8 M. Moreover, this is the first optical sensor capable 
of detecting Asp from solutions containing a variety of amino acids to date [152]. Li et al. 
used functionalized CIS/ZnS QDs as nanosensors in conjunction with acid phosphatase 
(ACP)-triggered  hydrolysis  of  ascorbic  acid-2-phosphate  (AAP)  to  ascorbic  acid  (AA) 
to  develop  a  novel  fluorescence-  and  colorimetric  dual-mode  ACP  activity  detection 
method. Highly sensitive ACP detection in the range of 0.22–12.5 U L− 1 was achieved by 
fluorescence “on” mode with a LOD of 0.064 U L− 1. In addition, the designed nanosen-
sors  are  biocompatible  and  can  be  successfully  used  for  imaging  and  monitoring  ACP 
levels  in  living  cells  [153].  Rasoulzadeh  et  al.  first  utilized  water-soluble  CIS  QDs  as  a 
chemiluminescent (CL) reagent and applied it to a highly sensitive diconazole assay. The

5  Conclusion

Under globally tightening environmental regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the 
WEEE  Directive,  eco-friendly  QDs  including  InP,  graphene,  and  CuInS₂  are  poised  to 
revolutionize  biomedical,  optoelectronic  sensing,  display,  and  energy-efficient  lighting 
industries. The innovation and advancement of these QDs align with the United Nations 
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  and  national  green  manufacturing  policies, 
establishing  regulatory  prerequisites  for  cross-industrial  adoption  of  environmentally 
compliant  nanomaterials.  Eco-friendly  QDs  exhibit  distinct  technological  advantages. 
For instance, InP QDs demonstrate tunable bandgaps (emission sizes of 2.5–3.7 nm) and 

He et al. Discover Nano          (2025) 20:132  
 Page 35 of 40

near-commercial  external  quantum  efficiency  (EQE > 15%  in  QLEDs),  thus  positioning 
them  as  RoHS-compliant  alternatives  for  next-generation  displays.  Graphene-derived 
QDs meet ISO 10,993 biocompatibility standards with cytotoxicity below 5% and mul-
timodal  imaging  capabilities.  Meanwhile,  CIS  QDs  achieve  60.1%  PLQY  using  low-
toxicity  precursors,  reducing  hazardous  waste  by  80%  compared  to  conventional  Cd/
Pb-based QDs synthesis. Since 2022, twelve eco-friendly QDs products have been certi-
fied under China’s GB/T 26,572 − 2021 standard. However, challenges persist in develop-
ing green QDs, such as QDs fluorescence imaging exhibits low sensitivity in deep-tissue 
in  vivo  applications,  while  metal-organic  chemical  synthesis  of  QD  nanocrystals  faces 
stringent  synthesis  conditions,  complex  reaction  protocols,  high  costs,  and  abundant 
surface defects.

6  Prospect

In the foreseeable future, with the continuous breakthroughs in eco-friendly QDs prepa-
ration technologies such as biological template synthesis and microwave-assisted prepa-
ration, coupled with the market forces driven by government green industry subsidies, 
environmental tax incentives, and other policies, the interplay and synergy of these two 
factors will strongly promote a profound transformation of the research paradigm in the 
field  of  nanotechnology. The  in-depth  exploration  of  cutting-edge  theories  by  the  aca-
demic community, the urgent need for technology transfer in the industrial sector, and 
the goal of policymakers to create a favorable development environment make strategic 
cooperation among the three parties the key to overcoming technical bottlenecks such 
as insufficient stability of QDs and difficulties in large-scale production. Specifically, by 
actively advancing the refinement of core-shell engineering to enhance the performance 
of QDs, deeply integrating the concept of circular economy to achieve efficient resource 
utilization  and  minimize  waste,  and  simultaneously  accelerating  the  unification  and 
standardization of regulatory standards, it is promising to establish a green and sustain-
able  nanotechnology  ecosystem.  This  ecosystem  will  not  only  strictly  comply  with  the 
increasingly stringent global environmental requirements but also bring transformative 
industrial applications to fields such as optoelectronic devices and biomedical imaging, 
reshaping  the  relevant  industrial  landscape  and  propelling  global  science,  technology, 
and industry towards a greener and more efficient future.

title: Promising biomedical applications using superparamagnetic nanoparticles

sections.heading: Synthesis methods of magnetic nanoparticles
sections.text: Synthesis methods of magnetic nanoparticles Nanoparticles (NPs) can be synthesized using two primary techniques: top-down and bottom-up approaches, as illustrated in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Synthesis techniques of nanoparticles The synthesis of MNPs is a critical factor influencing their size, shape, crystallinity, magnetic behavior, and biocompatibility [ 2 ]. Various methods have been developed to produce them with controlled physicochemical properties, broadly categorized into chemical, physical, and biological approaches; Fig.  2  [ 19 ]. Fig. 2 Methods for synthesizing various types of MNPs [ 19 ] Chemical methods Chemical synthesis is the most widely used approach for producing monodisperse, high-purity with tailored surface characteristics. Some of the most common chemical techniques include: Co-precipitation: A simple, cost-effective method where ferrous (Fe 2 ⁺) and ferric (Fe 3 ⁺) salts undergo precipitation in an alkaline medium, forming iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe₃O₄ or γ-Fe₂O₃) [ 20 ,  21 ].  Laurent  et al .  illustrated its efficacy in synthesizing superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) for MRI, highlighting the significance of pH and ionic strength in regulating particle size [ 22 ]. While scalable, it often results in polydisperse particles and requires post-synthesis modifications for enhanced stability. Thermal decomposition: Organometallic precursors decompose at high temperatures in organic solvents with surfactants, yielding highly crystalline and monodisperse nanoparticles [ 23 ]. Sun et al .  refined this methodology, attaining exact size control (4–20 nm) for Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles suitable for biological applications [ 24 ]. This method allows precise control over particle size and shape but involves complex synthesis conditions and organic solvents, limiting biocompatibility. Microemulsion: A surfactant-stabilized nanoscale reaction environment that controls nucleation and growth, producing uniform MNPs [ 25 ]. However, it has a low yield and requires extensive purification. Spinel ferrites are generated in microemulsions and inverse micelles. For example, MnFe 2 O 4  nanoparticles with diameters ranging from 4 to 15 nm are generated using water-in-toluene inverse micelles and NaDBS as a surfactant [ 26 ]. Sol–gel method: Involves the hydrolysis and condensation of metal precursors, producing highly stable magnetic nanostructures [ 27 ]. It is widely used for coating magnetic cores with silica or other protective layers. Ferrites like CoFe₂O₄ (15–40 nm) are produced with metal nitrates and citric acid, offering tunable magnetic properties after calcination at 600–800 °C [ 22 ]. Hybrid MNPs (e.g., Fe₃O₄@TiO₂, 20–60 nm) combine magnetic and photocatalytic traits [ 27 ]. Hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis: Conducted under high temperature and pressure in a sealed autoclave, yielding high-purity, crystalline nanoparticles with excellent colloidal stability [ 28 ]. Li et al .  synthesized monodisperse, hydrophilic, single-crystalline ferrite microspheres using hydrothermal reduction [ 29 ]. Wang et al. found that a 40-nm nanoscale Fe 3 O 4  powder can be made using the hydrothermal technique at 140 °C for 6 h, with a saturation magnetization of 85.8 emu. g −1  [ 30 ]. Electrochemical synthesis: Uses electrolysis of metal salts to generate nanoparticles with precise size and shape control but is limited by low production rates [ 31 ]. Physical methods Physical methods rely on energy-intensive techniques to produce MNPs by reducing bulk materials to nanoscale dimensions or directly forming nanoparticles from precursors [ 32 ]. These methods include: Ball milling: A mechanical grinding process that reduces bulk magnetic materials into nanosized particles [ 33 ,  34 ]. While scalable, it often leads to broad particle size distributions and irregular morphologies. For example, iron nanoparticles smaller than 50 nm have been created via prolonged milling of iron powder in an argon atmosphere [ 35 ]. Laser ablation: A high-energy laser beam vaporizes a metal target in a liquid or gas medium, forming pure, contaminant-free MNPs with controlled morphology [ 36 ]. For instance, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe₃O₄) with sizes ranging from 5 to 30 nm have been synthesized using pulsed laser ablation of an iron target in water, demonstrating high purity, superparamagnetic behavior, and suitability for biomedical applications such as MRI contrast enhancement and hyperthermia therapy [ 37 ]. Sputtering: A vacuum-based deposition method where high-energy ions bombard a target material, releasing nanoparticles with controlled thickness and structure [ 38 ]. Copper (Cu) nanoparticles, averaging 10–20 nm in size, were produced using DC magnetron sputtering. The resultant nanoparticles demonstrated elevated purity and a limited size distribution, making them appropriate for catalytic applications [ 39 ]. Biological methods Biological synthesis offers an eco-friendly, non-toxic approach for their synthesis using microorganisms, plant extracts, or biomolecules as reducing and stabilizing agents [ 40 ]. Microbial synthesis: Certain bacteria, such as  Magneto spirillum  species, naturally produce magnetosomes biogenic MNPs with precise size and shape control. These nanoparticles exhibit excellent biocompatibility and potential for medical applications [ 41 ].  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  produces extracellular iron oxide MNPs (10–30 nm) in iron-rich, carbon-minimal media at low pH, with magnetic alignment confirmed via external fields [ 40 ]. Plant-mediated synthesis: Plant extracts containing bioactive compounds (phenols, flavonoids, tannins) reduce metal precursors to form biocompatible and functionalized MNPs without toxic chemical reagents [ 42 ]. For example, zinc ferrite nanoparticles were synthesized using guava leaves extract for biomedical applications [ 1 ]. Enzyme-assisted synthesis: Enzymes such as laccases and reductases mediate MNP formation, allowing for highly controlled synthesis under mild conditions [ 43 ]. Nitrate reductases from microbial sources catalyze the reduction of Fe 3 ⁺ to Fe 2 ⁺, forming iron oxide MNPs (e.g., magnetite, Fe₃O₄) with sizes of 5–50 nm [ 43 ]. While hydrogenase enzymes from  Clostridium pasteurianum  reduce Fe 3 ⁺ intracellularly to form magnetite MNPs (~ 15 nm) [ 41 ].

sections.text: Biological methods Biological synthesis offers an eco-friendly, non-toxic approach for their synthesis using microorganisms, plant extracts, or biomolecules as reducing and stabilizing agents [ 40 ]. Microbial synthesis: Certain bacteria, such as  Magneto spirillum  species, naturally produce magnetosomes biogenic MNPs with precise size and shape control. meta.title: Promising biomedical applications using superparamagnetic nanoparticles

raw:
Introduction Nanoparticles (NPs) are materials characterized by at least one dimension within the nanometer scale, typically up to approximately 100 nm [ 1 ]. Due to their high surface-area-to-volume ratio, NPs exhibit unique physicochemical properties that differ from their bulk counterparts, making them highly versatile for various scientific and industrial applications [ 2 ]. Among these, MNPs have gained substantial attention due to their responsiveness to external magnetic fields, making them valuable in diverse fields such as biomedicine, catalysis, environmental remediation, and energy storage [ 3 ]. They are typically composed of metal-based structures, including iron, cobalt, nickel, titanium, and ferrite compounds like magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and maghemite (γ-Fe₂O₃). These materials exhibit superparamagnetic behavior, meaning they can rapidly transition between magnetic states upon exposure to an external magnetic field, driven by their magnetic moment and field properties, and lose their magnetization when the field is removed, behaving as nonmagnetic particles [ 4 ]. This property, along with their high specific absorption rate (SAR) under alternating magnetic fields (AMF), enables efficient heat generation for applications like hyperthermia therapy, enhancing treatment outcomes in cancer therapy through material composition and structural optimization [ 5 ,  6 ]. The physicochemical properties of these particles, including their size, surface charge, colloidal stability, and biocompatibility, significantly influence their potential applications [ 7 ]. While MNPs, such as iron oxide-based nanoparticles, exhibit inherent stability in physiological environments, modifications such as surface functionalization with biocompatible polymers (e.g., dextran, polyethylene glycol) or inorganic coatings (e.g., silica, gold) further enhance their stability, prevent aggregation, and optimize their interaction with biological systems[ 2 ]. Recent studies have demonstrated that optimizing colloidal stability through appropriate surface modifications prevents nanoparticle aggregation, ensuring their effective circulation in biological environments [ 8 ,  9 ]. Additionally, improving biocompatibility through functionalization minimizes immune system activation, reducing cytotoxic effects and enhancing therapeutic efficacy [ 10 ]. Beyond superparamagnetism, properties like high saturation magnetization and anisotropic behavior further dictate MNPs’ suitability for medical and industrial applications [ 11 ]. In biomedicine, magnetic nanoparticles have been extensively researched for their role in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast enhancement, targeted drug delivery, hyperthermia therapy, and biosensing [ 12 ]. Moreover, MNPs have shown significant promise in the field of theranostics, a rapidly evolving approach that integrates therapeutic and diagnostic capabilities into a single nanoscale platform. In this context, MNPs can be engineered to act both as imaging agents, such as contrast enhancers in MRI, and as therapeutic carriers for drug delivery or hyperthermia treatments [ 13 ]. The theranostic application of MNPs not only enhances treatment precision, but also minimizes systemic toxicity, making them a key component in the advancement of personalized and targeted medicine [ 14 ]. MNPs’ capacity to react to external magnetic fields facilitates accurate localization within the body, minimizing systemic adverse effects in therapeutic applications [ 15 ]. They have demonstrated significant potential in clinical medicine, particularly in targeted therapies for cancer treatment, neurological disorders, and infectious diseases [ 16 ]. Their use in hyperthermia therapy for cancer, where localized heating induced by alternating magnetic fields selectively destroys malignant cells, has shown promising results. Additionally, functionalized MNPs have facilitated advancements in drug delivery systems by enabling site-specific release and controlled drug administration [ 17 ]. Additional limitations or requirements are largely determined by the intended use of the MNPs, whether in vitro or in vivo. In vitro applications typically have fewer constraints compared to in vivo ones [ 18 ]. For magnetic structures, a biocompatible polymer coating is often essential if the nanoparticles lack inherent biocompatibility. This coating, applied during or after manufacturing, helps reduce toxicity, minimize the risk of blood capillary constriction, and prevent nanoparticle aggregation [ 2 ]. The continuous evolution of nanotechnology has paved the way for groundbreaking advancements in magnetic nanoparticle research. By refining synthesis methods, optimizing surface modifications, and enhancing biocompatibility, MNPs hold immense promise for revolutionizing biomedical applications. However, challenges related to large-scale production, toxicity, and regulatory approval must be addressed before their full clinical potential can be realized. This review explores the developments in MNP-based technologies, focusing on their synthesis, characterization, properties, and biomedical applications. Additionally, it highlights the challenges and future perspectives of integrating them into clinical practice, aiming to bridge the gap between laboratory research and real-world medical applications.

General structure of magnetic nanoparticles Magnetic nanoparticles consist of a magnetic core responsible for their magnetism and a protective surface layer that enhances stability, prevents aggregation, and allows for functionalization [ 44 ]. They can be synthesized from a variety of compositions and phases, encompassing pure metallic elements, metal oxides (e.g., Fe₃O₄, γ-Fe₂O₃), ferrites (e.g., BaFe₁₂O₁₉, SrFe₁₂O₁₉, and MFe₂O₄, where M represents divalent cations such as Cu, Ni, Mn, Mg), and metal alloys (e.g., CoPt, FePt). These nanoparticles exhibit either ferrimagnetic or superparamagnetic behavior, depending on their size and composition [ 48 ]. Cobalt ferrite (CoFe₂O₄) has high magnetic anisotropy and chemical stability, making it suitable for high-density data storage and magnetic sensors. Nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄) exhibits moderate magnetization and electrical conductivity, which makes it useful in biomedical imaging and catalysis. Manganese ferrite (MnFe₂O₄) has tunable magnetic properties and is often employed in drug delivery and hyperthermia applications. Zinc ferrite (ZnFe₂O₄) is a low-magnetization material commonly used in magnetic fluids and sensing devices. Ferrite nanoparticles are advantageous due to their stability, resistance to oxidation, and ability to be synthesized with controlled magnetic properties. To further enhance their performance, they are often coated with biopolymers, silica, or surfactants for improved dispersibility in aqueous environments [ 22 ]. These properties make them ideal for magnetic storage, electromagnetic shielding, and catalysis. However, pure metal nanoparticles are prone to oxidation and corrosion, necessitating protective coatings or alloying with more stable elements [ 49 ]. Below are examples of metallic magnetic nanoparticles. Iron nanoparticles possess strong ferromagnetic behavior, but are highly reactive to oxygen and moisture. They are often coated with carbon, silica, or noble metals to improve stability. Cobalt and nickel nanoparticles exhibit high coercivity and strong magnetic interactions but can be cytotoxic in biological applications, limiting their use unless encapsulated in inert coatings. Rare-earth magnetic materials, such as samarium–cobalt (SmCo) and neodymium–iron–boron (NdFeB), provide strong permanent magnetism, which is useful in industrial and electronic applications. Due to their superior magnetization properties, metallic nanoparticles are often used in high-performance applications but require surface modifications for practical use in biomedical or environmental settings [ 50 ]. Iron oxide nanoparticles Iron oxide-based NPs, including Fe₃O₄ and γ-Fe₂O₃, are commonly used due to their biocompatibility, superparamagnetic behavior, and stability in physiological environments. These materials have a spinel crystal structure, where oxygen ions form a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice while iron ions occupy both tetrahedral and octahedral sites. In Fe₃O₄, iron exists in a mixed Fe 2 ⁺/Fe 3 ⁺ state, whereas in γ-Fe₂O₃, Fe 3 ⁺ ions dominate, with some vacancies in the crystal lattice. These structural differences influence their magnetic response and oxidation resistance [ 46 ]. Iron oxide nanoparticles are frequently employed in MRI, drug delivery, and hyperthermia therapy due to their ability to be manipulated under an external magnetic field. However, they tend to form aggregates, which is why their surfaces are often modified with polymeric (PEG, dextran), inorganic (silica, gold), or biological (antibody, peptide) coatings to enhance dispersion and improve functionality [ 47 ].

Ferrite-based nanoparticles Ferrites are mixed metal oxides with the general formula MFe₂O₄, where M represents divalent cations such as manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), or zinc (Zn). These nanoparticles exhibit either ferrimagnetic or superparamagnetic behavior, depending on their size and composition [ 48 ]. Cobalt ferrite (CoFe₂O₄) has high magnetic anisotropy and chemical stability, making it suitable for high-density data storage and magnetic sensors. Nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄) exhibits moderate magnetization and electrical conductivity, which makes it useful in biomedical imaging and catalysis. Manganese ferrite (MnFe₂O₄) has tunable magnetic properties and is often employed in drug delivery and hyperthermia applications. Zinc ferrite (ZnFe₂O₄) is a low-magnetization material commonly used in magnetic fluids and sensing devices. Ferrite nanoparticles are advantageous due to their stability, resistance to oxidation, and ability to be synthesized with controlled magnetic properties. To further enhance their performance, they are often coated with biopolymers, silica, or surfactants for improved dispersibility in aqueous environments [ 22 ].

Advantages of magnetic nanoparticles in medical applications Size The biomedical efficacy of MNPs is closely linked to their dimensions, specifically two parameters: core size and hydrodynamic diameter (HD), which influence several functional aspects. The core size, usually assessed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), influences the magnetic characteristics of MNPs, including superparamagnetism and saturation magnetization, which are essential for applications such as hyperthermia treatment and MRI [ 11 ]. For example, MNPs with core diameters between 10 and 50 nm demonstrate excellent magnetic responsiveness, balancing robust magnetization and superparamagnetic properties to inhibit aggregation without an external magnetic field [ 54 ]. Conversely, the hydrodynamic diameter (HD), including the core and surface coatings (such as polymers or silica) and generally evaluated using dynamic light scattering (DLS) in physiological environments, dictates their pharmacokinetics and biodistribution in vivo [ 2 ]. In this section, size references relate to HD unless stated differently. MNPs having a hydrodynamic diameter (HD) between 10 and 100 nm provide an ideal equilibrium of extended circulation duration, effective cellular internalization, and advantageous biodistribution. Renew filtration swiftly eliminates parts with a hydrodynamic diameter of less than 10 nm, limiting their retention and therapeutic efficacy [ 55 ]. In contrast, particles larger than 200 nm are susceptible to detection and elimination by the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), especially in the liver and spleen, heightening the risk of accumulation and toxicity [ 56 ]. Nanoparticles with a 30 to 50 nm hydrodynamic diameter are superior for MRI contrast enhancement due to their substantial surface-area-to-volume ratio and increased relativity, enhancing imaging resolution [ 57 ]. In drug delivery, MNPs in the 50–100 nm range can efficiently penetrate biological barriers and leverage the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect to accumulate in tumor tissues while avoiding rapid immune clearance [ 15 ]. However, the EPR effect remains highly controversial, with some studies suggesting it may be overstated or even a fallacy in certain contexts due to tumor heterogeneity, inconsistent vascular permeability, and limited clinical translation in humans compared to preclinical models [ 58 ,  59 ]. Similarly, hyperthermia therapy benefits from particles sized 10–50 nm, as they demonstrate superior heat dissipation, efficiently converting electromagnetic energy into localized heating [ 60 ]. Additionally, surface modifications such as polymer or silica coatings can alter their hydrodynamic size, affecting their circulation and targeting efficiency. Precise control over nanoparticle size enables researchers to optimize pharmacokinetics, cellular interactions, and therapeutic efficacy, ensuring their safe and effective application across various medical fields [ 61 ]. Remote control functionality MNPs exhibit remote control functionality due to their ability to respond to external magnetic fields. This property allows for precise modulation of their movement and aggregation, which is particularly valuable in biomedical applications such as targeted drug delivery and biological labeling [ 62 ]. The interaction with external magnetic fields occurs through two key mechanisms: the gradient effect and alternating magnetic fields. The gradient effect relies on spatial variations in the magnetic field to guide them to specific locations within the body [ 63 ]. This targeted approach enhances drug delivery efficiency by concentrating therapeutic agents at the intended site while minimizing systemic exposure and side effects. Alternating magnetic fields, on the other hand, induce localized heating of MNPs, which can be leveraged for hyperthermia treatment in oncology. Additionally, the controlled movement of MNPs enables their application in precise biological labeling, where they can be guided to specific cells or tissues for imaging and diagnostic purposes [ 64 ]. Resonance reaction to field variations Under alternating magnetic fields (AMF), MNPs undergo rapid magnetization reversals, dissipating energy as heat for applications such as hyperthermia therapy [ 65 ]. This localized heating is a key mechanism in magnetic hyperthermia, selectively destroying cancerous cells while sparing healthy tissues [ 66 ]. The extent of this thermal effect is influenced by factors such as nanoparticle composition, size, and the frequency of the applied magnetic field. Beyond hyperthermia, resonance-based magnetic interactions are also being explored for applications in controlled drug release and enhanced imaging contrast in MRI diagnostics [ 67 ]. To contextualize these advantages, Table  1  compares MNPs with other nanoparticle types commonly used in biomedical applications.

Magnetic nanoparticle in drug delivery process MNPs play a crucial role in drug delivery by enabling precise targeting, controlled release, and enhanced therapeutic efficacy [ 68 ]. This section outlines the stages of MNP-based drug delivery, ensuring relevance to their biomedical applications. Drug loading Magnetic nanoparticles can be engineered with various coatings and functional groups to enhance drug loading efficiency and stability. Encapsulation strategies include covalent bonding, electrostatic interactions, and polymeric coatings, which prevent premature drug release and improve bioavailability [ 69 ]. Circulation and targeting Upon administration, MNPs travel through the bloodstream, with their distribution influenced by size, surface modifications, and interactions with biological components. Their ability to evade immune clearance is essential for prolonged circulation [ 70 ]. They reach target tissues via passive or active targeting mechanisms; Fig.  4  [ 71 ]. Fig. 4 Active and passive targeting of nanoparticles [ 71 ] Passive targeting: utilizes the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect to concentrate MNPs in tumour areas, attributed to compromised vasculature and inadequate lymphatic drainage [ 72 ]. The dependability of the EPR effect varies among tumor types, species, and stages, potentially overestimating its efficacy for metal-based nanoparticles. This method is significantly influenced by nanoparticle size, shape, and surface characteristics [ 61 ], but it often leads to generalized accumulation in the tumor microenvironment rather than selective uptake by malignant tumor cells [ 73 ]. Active targeting: Conversely, it enhances the precision of magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) drug delivery by using ligands such as antibodies, peptides, or small molecules that bind to specific receptors either on tumor cells or within the tumor microenvironment [ 74 ]. This approach can be categorized into tumor cell-specific targeting, which involves receptors overexpressed on malignant cells, and tumor tissue-specific targeting, which focuses on receptors located on nonmalignant cells such as endothelial or stromal cells within the tumor environment. For example, folic acid-functionalized MNPs bind to folate receptors commonly overexpressed on cancer cells, facilitating direct delivery to tumor cells [ 75 ]. In contrast, transferrin-coated MNPs target transferrin receptors on endothelial cells of the blood–brain barrier, promoting accumulation in brain tumor regions without directly targeting tumor cells [ 76 ]. Targeting integrins on tumor vasculature is another tissue-level strategy, promoting broader accumulation but potentially reducing cancer cell specificity. The distinction between these targeting types is vital: tissue-level targeting aids accumulation in the tumor microenvironment, while cell-level targeting ensures precise delivery to malignant cells. Challenges like ligand stability, receptor heterogeneity, and off-target binding can affect both strategies’ accuracy [ 77 ]. Controlled drug release and therapeutic action Magnetic nanoparticles enable precise drug release through external magnetic stimuli, utilizing various controlled release mechanisms. One approach is magnetic hyperthermia, where an alternating magnetic field generates localized heat, triggering drug release and inducing apoptosis in cancer cells. Another strategy involves pH-sensitive coatings that degrade in the acidic tumor microenvironment, ensuring site-specific drug activation. Additionally, enzyme-responsive systems rely on specific enzymatic activity at the disease site to initiate drug release, further enhancing targeted therapeutic efficacy [ 78 ]. Biocompatibility and clearance The biocompatibility and clearance of MNPs are essential considerations for their safe and effective clinical use. The mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS) plays a key role in recognizing and eliminating nanoparticles based on their size and surface characteristics. In the context of drug delivery, optimizing factors such as hydrodynamic diameter, surface charge, and coating materials (e.g., polyethylene glycol (PEG), dextran, or silica) is critical for minimizing immune recognition and improving systemic circulation [ 79 ]. Surface modifications help minimize opsonization, thereby decreasing MPS uptake and enhancing biodistribution. Neutral or slightly negative surface charges are generally associated with reduced macrophage internalization compared to positively charged particles, which tend to interact more strongly with cell membranes [ 80 ]. Advanced coatings such as zwitterionic polymers can further prevent protein corona formation and promote extended circulation times [ 81 ]. Additionally, the use of biodegradable materials supports safe elimination through renal or hepatic pathways, lowering the risk of long-term accumulation and associated toxicity [ 79 ]. These strategies underscore the importance of rational nanoparticle design to maximize biocompatibility and therapeutic performance.

Applications of magnetic nanoparticles in biomedical research Magnetic nanoparticles have a broad range of applications in biomedical research, demonstrating significant potential in areas such as medical imaging, targeted drug delivery, and regenerative medicine. Their ability to be guided and manipulated using external magnetic fields makes them valuable tools for precise and non-invasive therapeutic interventions; Fig.  5  [ 82 ]. Fig. 5 Applications of MNPs in biomedical research [ 82 ] Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) MNPs enable advanced MRI applications, including cancer imaging, in vivo tracking of iron oxide-doped stem cells, and monitoring transplanted tissue functionality, offering precise insights into disease progression and therapeutic outcomes [ 83 ]. The application of superparamagnetic magnetite nanocrystal clusters (SMNCs) in cellular imaging represents a valuable and versatile tool in biomedical research [ 84 ]. These SMNCs exhibit remarkable magnetic resonance sensitivity, maintain cell viability without adverse effects, and demonstrate properties that are both dose- and time-dependent [ 85 ,  86 ]. Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) have been extensively employed as tracers in preclinical models for the treatment of cardiovascular and central nervous system disorders [ 87 ]. Notably, iron oxide nanoparticles (IONPs) functionalized with polyethylene glycol (PEG) markedly improve blood circulation durations, diminish immune clearance, and facilitate extended MRI monitoring of biodistribution, essential for monitoring therapeutic administration and tissue targeting [ 87 ]. Zhao et al. investigated the viability and proliferation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells labeled with superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs). Their findings revealed that delivering cell transplants via liver or spleen injections could accelerate liver regeneration. Furthermore, in vivo MRI of SPIONs-labeled cells enables real-time monitoring of liver regeneration, offering valuable insights for clinical management post-hepatectomy [ 88 ]. Serve as magnetic hyperthermia agents [ 100 ] Magnetic nanoparticles in cancer therapy and chemotherapy Cancer poses a significant challenge to society, with a growing global incidence affecting millions of individuals [ 101 ]. Magnetic nanoparticles have emerged as powerful tools in cancer management, integrating targeted drug delivery, advanced imaging, and innovative therapies to improve outcomes [ 102 ]. In chemotherapy, MNPs enhance precision by conjugating anticancer agents such as doxorubicin, gemcitabine, or methotrexate to their surfaces, allowing external magnetic fields to guide them to tumor sites [ 103 ]. Modified with biocompatible coatings (e.g., dextran, polyethylene glycol), functional ligands, or antibodies, MNPs achieve selective interaction with malignant cells, facilitating controlled drug release via magnetic modulation, pH shifts, or enzymatic triggers [ 104 ]. In cancer chemotherapy, this approach enables sustained accumulation of anticancer drugs (e.g., doxorubicin) at tumor sites, enhances cellular uptake via receptor-mediated endocytosis, and reduces systemic toxicity, thereby improving therapeutic outcomes [ 74 ]. Beyond chemotherapy, MNPs enhance cancer diagnostics and imaging by leveraging their superparamagnetic properties to improve tumor visualization, aiding early detection and treatment planning [ 105 ]. Multifunctional MNPs enable a theranostic approach, combining therapy and real-time monitoring, as seen with platforms integrating drug delivery and MRI contrast enhancement. Additionally, they expand treatment options through gene therapy and immunotherapy, acting as vectors for genetic material or immune stimulants, offering alternatives to heat-based methods [ 106 ]. In contrast, advanced targeting strategies, such as glucuronic acid-functionalized iron oxide nanoparticles (IONPs) for glioblastoma, employ intravenous administration to exploit systemic circulation and GLUT-mediated transcytosis, augmented by moderate hypoglycemia, achieving unparalleled success in active targeting [ 124 ]. Intratumoral injection ensures high nanoparticle concentrations at the tumor site, enhancing heating efficiency and minimizing systemic exposure, but it is invasive and limited to accessible, localized tumors [ 125 ]. Magnetic nanoparticles in cancer therapy and chemotherapy Cancer poses a significant challenge to society, with a growing global incidence affecting millions of individuals [ 101 ]. However, ensuring their biocompatibility is crucial, as their potential cytotoxic effects could impact clinical safety. Several factors influence MNP cytotoxicity, including size, shape, surface chemistry, composition, dose, and exposure duration [ 2 ]. Smaller nanoparticles can penetrate cells more easily, potentially causing toxicity, while surface coatings and functional groups play a critical role in stability and immune interactions. The metal core and magnetic properties of MNPs can also contribute to cellular stress, and excessive aggregation may alter their biological interactions [ 80 ]. Notably, the route of administration (e.g., intravenous, inhalation, or topical) can further modulate these effects, as it determines the nanoparticles’ interaction with different biological barriers and tissues [ 162 ]. Oxidative stress occurs when reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and DNA damage [ 164 ]. Direct interactions with cell membranes can compromise structural integrity, while mitochondrial dysfunction may reduce ATP production and induce apoptosis. Additionally, They can trigger immune activation and inflammation, which may contribute to adverse effects at the tissue level [ 165 ]. For instance, uncoated iron oxide nanoparticles have been shown to induce higher ROS levels compared to polymer-coated variants, highlighting the protective role of surface modifications [ 166 ]. Challenges and future perspectives Magnetic nanoparticles hold great potential in biomedicine, environmental science, and advanced materials, but several challenges must be overcome for their full implementation. One major issue is the scalability and reproducibility of nanoparticle synthesis. While precise control over their properties is achievable in the lab, ensuring consistency in large-scale production remains complex. Developing cost-effective, high-yield methods that maintain uniformity is crucial for clinical and commercial applications. Additionally, improving nanoparticle stability through optimized surface coatings and functionalization techniques will enhance circulation time and therapeutic effectiveness. Biocompatibility and long-term safety are also critical concerns. Although iron oxide-based MNPs are generally considered safe, prolonged accumulation in organs such as the liver and spleen raise toxicity risks. Researchers are addressing this by developing biodegradable and excretable formulations that retain magnetic properties while being efficiently cleared from the body. Surface modifications with biocompatible materials can further improve interactions with biological systems and reduce immune responses. Standardized toxicity assessment protocols will be essential for regulatory approval. Another promising area is the development of multifunctional MNP platforms that integrate diagnostics and therapy. Combining magnetic targeting with imaging, photothermal therapy, or enzyme-mimetic activity could revolutionize personalized medicine. Hybrid nanoparticles with both plasmonic and magnetic components are being explored for dual-modal imaging and precision-targeted treatments. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) may further enhance real-time disease monitoring by improving MNP-based imaging and therapeutic accuracy. Beyond healthcare, MNPs are gaining attention in environmental and energy applications. Their high surface area and magnetic properties make them valuable for removing pollutants from water, while their potential in energy storage, catalysis, and electromagnetic shielding is being explored for next-generation batteries and electronics. Integrating MNPs with materials science and environmental engineering could lead to major advancements in sustainable technology. To translate these innovations into real-world applications, regulatory and clinical challenges must be addressed. Comprehensive studies on nanoparticle pharmacokinetics, long-term biodistribution, and metabolic pathways are necessary for establishing safety guidelines. Regulatory bodies require rigorous characterization protocols before approving MNP-based medical applications. Future efforts should focus on developing highly efficient, minimally toxic, and precision-targeted MNPs that meet safety and efficacy standards. Overcoming these challenges will enable the widespread adoption of MNPs in healthcare, environmental sustainability, and advanced materials.

Conclusion Magnetic nanoparticles are increasingly recognized as important medical tools, particularly for diagnostic and therapeutic applications. Their unique magnetic properties make them ideal contrast agents for MRI, enhancing image quality and aiding in the early detection of diseases by improving the visibility of tissues and abnormalities. SPIONs are widely used in clinical settings for liver imaging and angiography, demonstrating their effectiveness in diagnostic imaging. Additionally, MNPs enable targeted drug delivery by concentrating therapeutic agents in specific areas of the body, thereby minimizing adverse effects. This magnetic drug-targeting approach enhances treatment efficacy by delivering medications precisely to the required locations, particularly in cancer therapy. Surface coatings can further improve targeting efficiency and biocompatibility by modifying the physical and chemical properties of the particles. Additionally, magnetic thermoablation utilizes nanoparticles to generate localized heat in specific tissues, providing a novel approach for cancer treatment. These applications highlight the versatility of MNPs in advancing both medical diagnostics and therapeutic interventions, contributing to the development of more effective and minimally invasive treatments.
