Nucleic acid detachment reaction on the surface 
of nanomaterials
The detachment of NAs from nanomaterial surfaces is a 
key  focus  in  numerous  studies  and  applications.  Selec-
tive  detachment  and  detection  of  specific  DNA  or  RNA 
sequences  are  crucial  for  diagnosing  genetic  diseases, 
identifying  pathogens,  and  monitoring  gene  expression 
[134].  In  drug  delivery,  nanomaterials  act  as  carriers  for 

NA-based  therapies,  enhancing  therapeutic  payloads 
while  minimizing  off-target  effects.  Controlled  release 
of NAs at target sites improves efficacy and reduces sys-
temic  side  effects  [7].  A  thorough  understanding  of  the 
methods and factors influencing NA detachment is vital 
for  developing  advanced  nanomaterial-based  platforms 
in  biomedical  and  biotechnological  applications.  Con-
tinued  exploration  of  novel  detachment  strategies  and 
elucidation  of  their  underlying  mechanisms  will  drive 
progress in the field, paving the way for innovative appli-
cations.  This  section  examines  common  types  of  NA 
detachment  reactions  on  nanomaterial  surfaces,  high-
lighting their advantages and limitations. Further details 
are summarized in Table 3.

tions  between  NAs  and  nanomaterials  (Fig.  1c)[135,  138]. 
For instance, urea or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) can dena-

[136,  153].  Magnetic  beads  modified  with  silanol  or  car-
boxyl  groups  create"salt"or"electrostatic  bridges"with  NAs. 
Tris–EDTA or phosphate buffers disrupt these interactions 
by lowering the salt concentration or increasing pH, which 
induces repulsion between the negatively charged NAs and 
the beads (Fig. 5b)[137, 154, 155]. For metallic nanomateri-
als, such as AuNPs, chemical destabilizers like dithiothreitol 
(DTT) can cleave Au–S bonds, effectively detaching conju-
gated  NAs  (Fig.  5c)[139].  Additionally,  potassium  cyanide 
(KCN) can solubilize metallic nanomaterials directly, facili-
tating complete release of bound NAs (Fig. 5d)[141].

The use of complementary DNA (cDNA) to detach NAs 
from  nanomaterial  surfaces  is  classified  as  a  chemical 
method.  Since  ssDNA  and  dsDNA  have  different  affinities 
for  nanomaterial  surfaces,  cDNA-mediated  displacement 
reactions  can  promote  the  release  of  fluorescently  labeled 
NAs [141, 142]. In this process, single-stranded fluorescent 
probes  initially  adsorbed  onto  nanomaterial  surfaces  are 
quenched due to their proximity. cDNA, complementary to 
the single-stranded probes, forms double- or triple-stranded 
DNA  structures  away  from  the  surface,  restoring  fluores-
cence. Based on this principle, many interesting nanomate-
rial-based direct nucleic acid detection platforms have been 
developed (Fig. 5e-f) [143, 156]. Further systematic investi-
gation  of  cDNA-induced  detachment  of  probe  DNA  from 
GO  surfaces  proposed  several  mechanisms  (Fig.  5g):  (1) 
Langmuir–Hinshelwood  model:  cDNA  adsorbs,  diffuses, 
hybridizes with probe DNA, and desorbs in two phases. (2) 
Eley–Rideal  model:  cDNA  hybridizes  directly  with  probe 
DNA  without  adsorbing.  (3)  Displacement  model:  cDNA 
replaces  probe  DNA  in  the  solution  and  hybridizes  with 
another  cDNA.  (4)  Surface  Heterogeneity:  Probe  DNA 

adsorbed  to  GO  with  varying  affinities  may  follow  one  or 
both  of  the  above  mechanisms  [144,  157].  Despite  these 
insights,  the  mechanisms  underlying  DNA  desorption  via 
strand displacement remain complex and subject to ongoing 
debate. Experimental evidence suggests that no single model 
fully accounts for all observed detachment phenomena. Fur-
ther  research  is  required  to  quantitatively  elucidate  these 
processes and improve our understanding of DNA desorp-
tion mechanisms.

Stimuli-responsive  NA  detachment  strategies  enable 
controlled  release  of  nucleic  acids  from  nanomateri-
als under specific external stimuli like pH and UV light, 
through  designed  surface  chemistry.  In  pH-responsive 
systems (Fig. 5h), DNA release is achieved by using pH-
sensitive sequences (e.g., i-motif, triplex) [145, 158, 159], 
or by breaking acid-labile bonds (e.g., hydrazone, ketal)/
protonating  surface  groups  (e.g.,  amines,  carboxyls)  on 
nanomaterials [146, 160, 161]. In UV-responsive systems 
(Fig. 5i), DNA release relies on photolabile linkers or pho-
toisomerization.  For  example,  DNA  linked  to  positively 
charged AuNPs via photolabile nitrobenzyl ester bonds is 
released upon UV irradiation (> 350 nm) [147]. Similarly, 
Ortho-nitrobenzyl  (ONB)-functionalized  nucleic  acids 
can partially release from nanomaterials under UV light 
[148]. Additionally, azobenzene-modified DNA on nano-
particles is released when UV converts azobenzene to its 
cis  form,  facilitating  its  detachment  from  the  cyclodex-
trin cavity [162, 163].

examined  the  kinetics  of  DNA  detachment  from  AuNP

The  excellent  photothermal  conversion  efficiency  of 
AuNPs  has  enabled  advanced  methods  for  light-stimu-
lated detachment of NAs. Research has shown that near-
infrared  (NIR)  light  can  detach  DNA  from  AuNRs  by 
generating’hot  electrons’that  cleave  Au–S  bonds  [166]. 
Similarly,  AuNRs  absorb  light,  causing  localized  heating 
that unwinds and releases DNA without significantly rais-
ing  the  solution’s  temperature,  indicating  a  non-thermo-
dynamic  mechanism  [167,  168].  Additionally,  the  effects 
of  continuous  wave  (CW)  and  femtosecond  pulse  lasers 
on  DNA  release  from  gold  nanoparticle  complexes  were 
different. CW lasers caused photothermal release of dehy-
bridized  ssDNA  while  the  complementary  strand  stayed 
bound.  Femtosecond  pulse  lasers  generated  non-equilib-
rium  hot  electrons,  breaking  Au–S  bonds  and  releasing 
intact dsDNA (Fig. 6b)[151]. Another study with different 

conclusions noted that silicon core/Au nanoshells irradi-
ated with near-infrared pulsed laser and continuous laser 
released  single-  and  double-stranded  NAs,  but  pulsed 
irradiation resulted in higher dsNA release [169]. The size 
and shape of nanomaterials significantly affect the release 
process.  Smaller  AuNPs  release  ssDNA  more  rapidly 
than  larger  particles  (Fig.  6c)  [165].  AuNRs  demonstrate 
more efficient siRNA release than Hollow gold nanoshells 
(HGNS)  or  Hollow  gold  nanocages  (HGNC)  when  sub-
jected  to  800  nm  pulsed  laser  excitation  (Fig.  6d)[152]. 
In  summary,  light-stimulated  NA  detachment  using  the 
plasmonic properties of metal nanoparticles offers precise 
control  over  release  by  tuning  the  wavelength,  intensity, 
and  irradiation  mode  of  light.  Additionally,  the  inher-
ent  characteristics  of  nanomaterials  and  the  type  of  NA 
conjugation significantly influence detachment outcomes 
[170].

Detaching NAs from nanomaterial surfaces is complex, 
influenced  by  factors  like  nanomaterial  size,  shape,  sur-
face  features,  and  environmental  conditions.  Advances 
in  light-responsive  and  strand  displacement  nanomate-
rials  enable  precise  NAs  release.  Hybrid  structures  and 
environmental  triggers  also  enhance  responsiveness  to

Nucleic acid signal amplification reaction 
on the Nanomaterials Surface
Signal  amplification  on  nanomaterial  surfaces  holds 
significant  potential  for  achieving  high  sensitivity  and 
selectivity in the in situ detection of NAs, thanks to its 
rapid  analytical  process  and  ease  of  miniaturization 
[171].  In  this  section,  we  divide  the  NA  signal  ampli-
fication  reactions  that  occur  on  the  surface  of  nano-
materials  into  enzyme-mediated  signal  amplification 
(nucleic  acid  amplification)  and  enzyme-free  signal 
amplification (HCR and CHA), as well as DNA Walker 
that enables signal amplification in both enzymatic and 
enzyme-free systems (Fig. 7).

Enzyme‑mediated nucleic acid amplification reaction

Nucleic acid amplification reactions (NAAR) are enzyme-
mediated  molecular  biotechnologies  used  to  replicate 
NAs  within  specific  systems  [172].  Nanomaterials  have 
been  integrated  into  NAAR  development  since  its  early 
stages,  with  nanomaterial-assisted  PCR  (nano-PCR) 
demonstrating  enhanced  amplification  sensitivity,  speci-
ficity, and efficiency (Fig. 7a)[173, 174]. Using AuNPs as 
a representative case, the introduction of optimal AuNP 
concentrations  into  NAAR  systems  induces  substantial 
interfacial  interactions  between  nanomaterial  surfaces 
and key components, including DNA polymerases, dou-
ble-stranded templates, single-stranded primers, salt ion 
buffers, and magnesium ions [175]. Lou et al. systemati-
cally  investigated  the  interactions  between  AuNPs  and 
PCR  components,  revealing  dynamic  adsorption–des-
orption processes of these components on AuNP surfaces 
during  thermal  cycling.  The  mechanism  is  threefold:

[176].  Sedighi  et  al.  demonstrated  that  AuNPs  preferen-

(HDA),  enhancing  DNA  unwinding  and  subsequently 
improving  amplification  speed  and  sensitivity  [177]. 
Our  previous  studies  corroborate  these  findings,  reveal-
ing  that  AuNPs  establish  energy  barriers  to  optimize 
nucleic  acid  interactions,  thereby  boosting  amplification 
sensitivity  [178].  Although  physicochemical  properties 
vary among nanomaterials, their common characteristic 
of  high  surface-to-volume  ratios  universally  enhances 
nucleic acid molecular interactions. Table 4 summarizes 
the influence of various nanomaterials on NAAR, catego-

In addition, the rational design of nanomaterial-medi-
ated nucleic acid (NA) amplification systems is essential 
for practical implementation. For instance, excessive gold 
nanoparticle  (AuNP)  concentrations  (>  1  nM)  suppress 

NA  amplification,  whereas  optimal  concentrations  (0.4 
nM)  significantly  enhance  amplification  efficiency  [174]. 
Larger  AuNPs  are  more  inhibitory  to  PCR  than  smaller 
ones at the same concentration [194]. Primers containing 
palindrome  sequences  (GGA TCC   or  ACC GGT ),  when 
combined  with  60  nm  AuNPs,  demonstrate  remarkable 
enhancement in quantitative real-time PCR amplification 
performance  [195].  Polyvinylpyrrolidone  (PVP)-mod-
ified  and  methoxy  polyethylene  glycol  thiol  (mPEG-
SH)-modified  AuNPs  exhibit  no  interference  with  PCR, 
whereas PDDA- and CTAB-functionalized particles may 
demonstrate  inhibitory  effects  on  the  reaction  [196]. 
Ongoing  research  focused  on  optimizing  nanomaterial 
physicochemical properties and surface functionalization 
strategies  will  drive  technological  innovations,  thereby 
providing more efficient and precise solutions for nucleic 
acid amplification and detection.

Colorimetric  detection  in  HCR/CHA  systems  can  be 
divided  into  two  methods.  The  first  involves  attaching 
DNA  initiators  to  nanomaterials,  triggering  HCR/CHA 
and  causing  nanomaterial  aggregation,  which  changes 
color  visibly  [199].  For  instance,  when  target  DNA 
opens  a  hairpin,  it  hybridizes  with  a  complementary 
sequence  on  AuNPs,  causing  aggregation  and  a  color 
shift [200]. This method was used for detecting miRNA-
21,  ATP,  thrombin,  and  acetylcholinesterase  activity 
[201,  202].  The  second  method  uses  DNA  polymers 
from  HCR/CHA  as  conjugates  with  nanomaterials  that 
mimic  peroxidase  activity,  catalyzing  substrates  like 
3,3’,5,5’-Tetramethylbenzidine  (TMB)  or  2,  2’-azino-
bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic  acid)  (ABTS)  with 
H₂O₂ to produce a color change [203, 204].

Fluorescence  detection  in  HCR/CHA  systems  mainly 
follows  two  approaches.  The  first  involves  using  nano-
materials  to  quench  fluorescence  by  adsorbing  labeled 
hairpins.  When  a  target  molecule  triggers  HCR/CHA, 
the hairpins open, restoring fluorescence [205, 206]. For 
instance, Miao et al. used a GO/Au nanocluster system to 
detect Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1), where AFB1 weakened hair-
pin adsorption on graphene oxide, allowing fluorescence 
recovery  for  detection  [207].  Similarly,  Li  et  al.  detected 
microRNAs  (miRNAs)  by  fluorescence  generated  by  a 
local  CHA  on  AuNPs  [208].  The  second  approach  uses 
nanomaterials  to  alter  fluorescence  by  interacting  with 
HCR/CHA products [209]. He et al. developed a method 
to detect the tumor biomarker transmembrane glycopro-
tein mucin 1(MUC1) using HCR with luminescent ruthe-
nium (II) complexes and CdZnTeS quantum dots. MUC1 
initiated  HCR  to  form  long  dsDNA  attached  to  MNPs. 
Ruthenium (II) complexes embedded in the dsDNA were 
magnetically separated, leaving minimal complexes in the 
supernatant and causing negligible fluorescence quench-
ing  of  the  QDs.  Significant  quenching  occurred  when 

complexes remained [210]. Similarly, Zhang et al. devel-
oped  a  miRNA-10b  detection  sensor  based  on  target-
triggered  CHA  signal  amplification  and  Luminescence 
resonance  energy  transfer  (LRET)  between  UCNPs  and 
AuNPs [211].

In  SERS  detection,  nanomaterials  like  AuNPs  and  Sil-
ver  nanoparticles  (AgNPs)  are  linked  with  organic  dyes 
through biotin-avidin interactions or nucleic acid hybrid-
ization  to  serve  as  Raman  signal  probes  for  quantifying 
target substances [212, 213]. Systems using nanoparticles 
with HCR/CHA achieve high sensitivity, detecting as low 
as  femtomolar  levels  and  even  single  cells.  For  instance, 
a  SERS  biosensor  combining  gold  Nanowires  (AuNWs), 
silver  staining,  and  HCR  was  developed  for  ultra-sensi-
tive miRNA detection, achieving a detection limit of 0.03 
fM [214]. A CHA and SERS-based dual signal amplifica-
tion  method  was  developed  for  the  simultaneous  detec-
tion of miRNA-21 and miRNA-155 with detection limits 
of 77 aM and 93 aM, respectively [215].

DNA walker on the surface of nanomaterials

DNA walkers are nanomachines made of DNA that move 
autonomously along a DNA track using a driving force, a 
walking chain, and a track. Activation of the driving force 
disrupts equilibrium, converting energy into motion and 
propelling the walker. Consuming fuel molecules restores 
equilibrium and generates a signal, which can be ampli-
fied  through  repeated  cycles  [216,  217].  This  unique 
movement  and  signal  amplification  make  DNA  walkers 
valuable for target detection and biological analysis, often 
enhanced  by  nanomaterials  like  AuNPs  and  MNPs  that 
stabilize  and  facilitate  their  movement  (Fig.  7c)  [218–
221].  DNA  walkers  can  be  categorized  by  their  driving 
force into enzymatic and non-enzymatic reactions.

Enzymatic  reactions  harness  restriction  endonucle-
ases,  exonucleases,  and  DNAzymes  to  act  on  the  DNA 
phosphate  backbone,  using  the  energy  from  covalent 
bond cleavage to drive DNA walker movement [222]. As 
shown  in  Fig.  7d,  the  process  includes:  (1)  DNA  walker 
attachment  to  the  track  via  complementary  pairing;  (2) 
enzyme recognition of a specific site on the DNA walker; 
(3)  enzyme-mediated  cutting  or  extension  of  the  DNA 
chain to release the walker; and (4) walker movement to 
an adjacent site based on enzyme action direction. These 
reactions  offer  high  catalytic  efficiency  and  specificity, 
facilitating  rapid  and  precise  DNA  walker  movement. 
For  instance,  Cheng  et  al.  developed  a  Flap  endonucle-
ase  1  (FEN  1)-powered  DNA  walker  for  mutant  DNA 
detection. The target DNA binds to the DNA track on the 
AuNP surface, enabling FEN 1 to cleave the overlapping 
DNA  track  chain,  generating  a  fluorescent  signal  and 
enhancing signal amplification [223].

Non-enzymatic  reactions 

include  strand  displace-
ment reactions (Fig. 7e) and environmentally responsive 
reactions  (Fig.  7f ).  Strand  displacement  reactions  are 
based  on  the  principle  of  strict  complementary  pairing 
in  DNA  double  strands,  enabling  DNA  strand  displace-

de-hybridization  between  the  walking  strand  and  the 
substrate  or  fuel  strand  [224].  Jiang  et  al.  designed  an 
enzyme-free  three-dimensional  DNA  walker  that  uses 
hairpin  catalytic  assembly  to  facilitate  its  movement 
[225].  Environmentally  responsive  reactions  are  driven 
by chemical agents (e.g.,  H+/OH−,  Hg2+/cysteine) or light 
stimuli, which interact with the DNA walker or track to 
propel  its  movement  [226].  Xian  et  al.  developed  a  NIR 
light-regulated  DNA  walker  system  that  uses  UCNPs  to 
convert  NIR  light  into  ultraviolet  light,  initiating  DNA 
walker movement for precise biological imaging [227].

Application of nucleic acid reactions 
on the nanomaterials surface for biomedicine
The  seamless  integration  of  NAs  with  nanomaterials 
has  unlocked  numerous  applications  in  the  biomedical 
field,  attributed  to  their  exceptional  biocompatibility 
and  stability.  In  this  section,  we  explore  several  key 
application  areas  arising  from  the  interactions  of  NAs 
on  nanomaterial  surfaces  and  highlight  representative 
examples.

NAs‑guided nanomaterial synthesis and assembly

Nucleic  acid-based  conjugation  with  nanomaterials  has 
greatly  advanced  precision  assembly  of  nanomaterials. 
NAs  act  as  templates  for  controlled  synthesis,  allowing 
precise  regulation  of  nanoparticle  size  and  shape,  and 
imparting  unique  properties.  Thiol-modified  ssDNA 
or  poly  A/C/G/T  chains  have  been  used  to  shape  metal 
nanocrystals. Specifically, ssDNA with 30 cytosine (C30) 
or adenine (A30) units turned spherical AuNP seeds into 
stable,  spiky  nanoflowers,  while  thymine-based  DNA 
(T30)  formed  spherical  nanoparticles  (Fig.  8a)[228]. 
Similarly, Different DNA sequences affect the shape and

A10 and -T10 convert nanocubic seeds into stellate octa-
hedral AgNPs with different truncations. Poly-oligo-C10 

produces  truncated  tetrahedral  AgNPs,  while  oligo-G10 
maintains the cubic shape and size of the AgNPs (Fig. 8b)
[229].

For  instance,  ssDNA  can  wrap  CNTs  and  integrate

Nanoplatforms of nucleic acid therapeutics

The  conjugation  and  detachment  of  nucleic  acids  on 
nanomaterials are crucial processes in nucleic acid thera-
peutics. Nucleic acid drugs, including DNA, miRNA, and 
siRNA, must enter cells to function effectively. However, 
their  large  molecular  size  and  negative  charge  lead  to 
repulsion  against  the  cell  membrane’s  lipid  bilayer,  hin-
dering their entry into cells [235]. Spherical nucleic acids 
(SNAs),  synthesized  by  conjugating  oligonucleotides  to 
nanoparticles, represent a promising platform for nucleic 
acid delivery, attributed to their distinctive three-dimen-
sional  architecture  [236,  237].  SNAs  are  composed  of 
densely  functionalized  and  highly  oriented  nucleic  acids 
on  the  surface  of  a  nanoparticle.  Since  the  properties 
of  SNAs  originate  from  their  nucleic  acid  shell,  diverse 
core  materials  can  be  employed,  including  metal  nano-
particles (e.g., Au, Pt), liposomes, and polymers (Fig. 9a)
[238]. SNAs exhibit low immunogenicity, enable reagent-
free transfection, and possess the capability to cross bio-
logical  barriers,  such  as  the  blood–brain  barrier  [238]. 
Covalent  coupling  stands  as  an  effective  strategy  for 
immobilizing nucleic acids on the surface of nanomateri-
als, such as conjugating nucleic acids to gold nanoparti-
cles  via  thiol  groups  [239].  However,  given  the  negative 
charge  of  siRNA,  non-covalent  electrostatic  interactions 
are  frequently  employed  as  an  alternative.  For  instance, 
nitrogen-doped  graphene  quantum  dots  can  directly 
bind  to  siRNA  [240].  Typically,  nanomaterial  surfaces 
are modified with molecules like PEI and PDDA to alter 
their surface charge from negative to positive [241, 242]. 
Nevertheless,  these  modifications  may  compromise  bio-
compatibility,  thereby  necessitating  the  development  of 
improved strategies. For instance, tyrosine-modified PEI 
and PEGylated PEI coatings can enhance both efficiency 
and biocompatibility [243, 244].

Once stable SNAs have successfully translocated across 
the target cell membrane, the subsequent detachment of

Commonly  employed  nucleic  acid  detachment  mecha-
nisms  encompass  reduction,  enzymatic  cleavage,  pH 
sensitivity,  and  photo-stimulation  (Fig.  9b)[245].  The 
choice  of  an  appropriate  release  strategy  depends  on 
the  stimulus-responsive  design  of  the  delivery  system. 
For  instance,  disulfide  bonds  enable  reduction-sensitive 
nanocarriers to release nucleic acid drugs in response to 
cellular  reductants  [248].  Polycationic  micellar  nucleic 
acid  carriers,  which  rely  on  electrostatic  interactions 
and  are  coated  with  thiolated  hyaluronic  acid,  facilitate 
the  delivery  of  plasmids  in  the  presence  of  hyaluroni-
dase-mediated  degradation  [249].  Imine  bonds  and  pH-
sensitive  coatings  introduced  into  PEGylated  liposomes 
enable  targeted  delivery  of  chemotherapeutic  and  gene 
therapy agents to tumors [250]. pH-sensitive nanomateri-
als, including metal–organic frameworks, quantum dots, 
and micelles, are capable of directly releasing gene drugs 
[251]. The exceptional photothermal properties of AuNPs 
facilitate  the  light-induced  release  of  nucleic  acids, 

thereby  promoting  significant  restoration  of  target  gene 
expression  [147].  Moreover,  the  system  design  permits 
the integrated control of siRNA release through multiple 
mechanisms. Yi et al. developed a Matrix metalloprotein-
ase-2 (MMP-2)-responsive immunotherapy that releases 
siRNA via reduction and enzymatic cleavage-stimulation 
(Fig. 9c)[246]. Gao et al. created a pH/reduction-respon-
sive  polycation  for  delivering  Multidrug  resistance  gene 
1  (MDR1)  siRNA  and  doxorubicin  to  combat  multidrug 
resistance (Fig. 9d)[247]. While multi-stimuli-responsive 
nanocarriers  are  promising,  it’s  unclear  if  their  benefits 
outweigh  the  associated  complexity.  Through  compre-
hensive  investigation  of  nucleic  acid  conjugation  and 
detachment  reactions  on  nanomaterial  surfaces,  it  is 
anticipated  that  more  efficient  and  intelligent  stimulus-
responsive  nanoparticles  will  soon  demonstrate  their 
clinical utility.

NA  conjugation  reactions  form  the  foundation  for 
constructing  robust  and  highly  specific  biosensors.  NA 
probes are securely anchored to the surface of nanomate-
rials through covalent and non-covalent coupling strate-
gies.  This  anchoring  prevents  probe  detachment  during 
detection and enhances biosensor stability. The high spe-
cific surface area of nanomaterials significantly increases 
probe  loading  density,  thereby  ensuring  efficient  target 
molecule  capture  by  each  detection  unit  and  enhanc-
ing  the  biosensor’s  directional  identification  capability. 
Moreover,  the  surface  modification  of  nanomaterials 

participating  in  the  conjugation  reaction,  such  as  PEG 
and Polyacrylic acid (PAA), reduces non-specific adsorp-
tion  in  complex  biological  samples,  thereby  enhancing 
the  detection  accuracy  of  biosensors  [252].  NA  detach-
ment reactions are essential for developing dynamic bio-
sensors. By utilizing competitive and stimulus-responsive 
detachment  processes,  targets  can  dynamically  modu-
late  the  binding  and  dissociation  equilibrium  between 
nucleic  acids  and  nanomaterials.  This  modulation  can 
induce  rapid  alterations  in  the  optical  and  electrical 
properties of nanomaterials. For instance, when a target 
binds more strongly to the nanomaterial’s surface nucleic 
acid  than  to  the  nanomaterial  itself,  the  nucleic  acid 
detaches, rapidly changing the solution’s color (Fig. 10a)
[253].  This  dynamic  reversibility  also  enables  sensor 
reuse,  significantly  reducing  inspection  costs  [254].  NA 
signal  amplification  reactions  are  pivotal  in  transcend-
ing  the  detection  sensitivity  thresholds  of  biosensors.

Leveraging  enzymatic  amplification  techniques  (e.g., 
PCR and isothermal nucleic acid amplification), enzyme-
free  self-assembly  methods  (e.g.,  HCR  and  CHA),  and 
the  synergistic  enhancement  provided  by  nanomateri-
als within cascade amplification effects, a singular target 
binding event can be converted into a detectably ampli-
fied signal of exponential magnitude [255]. The combined 
efforts  of  the  three  have  accelerated  the  development  of 
many cutting-edge biosensors in the field of biomedicine. 
For instance, surface coupling of magnetic nanoparticles 
with  capture  nucleic  acids  for  target  enrichment  ena-
bles  the  construction  of  electrochemical  biosensors  for 
miRNA detection following magnetic dissociation or sig-
nal  amplification  (Fig.  10b)[256].  Quenched  fluorescent 
probes  non-covalently  adsorbed  on  graphene  surfaces 
can  be  restored  to  fluorescence  by  the  target’s  rolling 
circle  amplification  products,  enabling  single-cell  imag-
ing  (Fig.  10c)[257].  AgNPs  coated  with  biotin-streptavi-
din  coupled  single  guide  RNA  (sgRNA)  can  trigger  the 
CRISPR/dCas9  signal  amplification  system,  construct-
ing  a  surface-enhanced  Raman  scattering  biosensor  for 

gene  mutation  detection  (Fig.  10d)[258].  Similar  strate-
gies  have  also  been  employed  to  construct  biosensors 
for detecting bacterial pathogens and cancer biomarkers 
[259,  260].  As  materials  science  and  molecular  biology 
become  increasingly  integrated,  biosensor  development 
is  expected  to  accelerate  toward  enhanced  portability, 
intelligence, and multifunctionality.

Challenges and perspectives
Despite extensive research into nucleic acid interactions 
with nanomaterial surfaces, significant challenges remain 
in  the  field.  Variations  in  the  size,  shape,  and  surface 
properties  of  nanomaterials  introduce  heterogeneity, 
complicating 
the  assurance  of  reaction  specificity 
and  reproducibility.  Structural  alterations  of  NAs  on 
nanomaterial  surfaces—such  as  folding,  aggregation,  or 
fragmentation—can  impair  target  binding  and  reduce 
reaction efficiency. Optimizing coupling and dissociation 
reactions  requires  precise  control  of  environmental 
factors, including pH, temperature, and ionic strength.

Biocompatibility  is  another  critical  concern,  as  nano-

must  be  minimized.  While  current  research  often

rial  surfaces  generate  complex  datasets,  encompassing 
thermodynamic and kinetic parameters. This complexity 
demands  multidimensional  analysis  and  diverse  analyti-
cal  techniques,  necessitating  interdisciplinary  expertise 
and effective communication among researchers.

Conclusions
In  summary,  this  review  explores  the  prevailing  meth-
odologies  for  conjugating  NAs  to  nanomaterial  surfaces 
and their subsequent detachment in response to external 
stimuli.  It  also  provides  an  in-depth  analysis  of  nucleic 
acid  signal  amplification  mechanisms  on  nanomaterial 
surfaces,  including  enzyme-mediated  signal  amplifica-
tion, enzyme-free signal amplification, and DNA Walker. 
The specific recognition properties of NAs, when syner-
gistically  integrated  with  the  versatile  and  robust  signal 
transduction capabilities of nanomaterials, make surface-
functionalized  nanomaterials  highly  suitable  for  both 
in vitro and in vivo nanomedicine applications.

NAs  conjugation  reactions  on  nanomaterial  surfaces 
can be broadly classified into covalent and non-covalent 
interactions. Covalent conjugation relies on pre-modified 
NAs  or  nanomaterials  linked  via  chemical  cross-linking 
agents,  forming  stable  complexes  ideal  for  long-term 
storage  and  in  vivo  delivery.  Non-covalent  conjugation, 
by  contrast,  uses  weaker  intermolecular  forces—such  as 
hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, and electrostatic 
interactions—offering  enhanced  biocompatibility  and 
safety,  though  with  reduced  stability.  NAs  detachment 
from  nanomaterial  surfaces  can  be  achieved  through 
physical  or  chemical  methods.  Physical  methods,  such 

as  heating  and  laser  techniques,  desorb  NAs  by  altering 
the  surface  energy  state  or  nanomaterial  properties. 
Chemical  methods  employ  replacement  chains  or 
specific  chemicals  to  modulate  adsorption  equilibrium, 
facilitating  the  detachment  process.  In  amplification 
reactions, particular emphasis is placed on the adsorption 
of amplification components onto nanomaterial surfaces. 
This  creates  a  concentrated  microenvironment  that 
enhances  specificity,  sensitivity,  and  efficiency.  In  HCR/
CHA,  nanomaterials  primarily  act  as  signal  amplifiers, 
categorized  into  colorimetric,  fluorescence,  and  SERS 
detection methods. In DNA walkers, nanomaterials serve 
critical roles as carriers, signal amplifiers, and facilitators

Materials and methods
Conductive nanoparticles, including silver32, can be created inside the graphene structure using various synthesis 
methods.  However,  in  this  paper,  the  sputtering  method  was  used  to  maintain  the  economical,  simple,  and 
scalable process, in addition to fabricating the sensor to improve it.

This paper used a laser method to form a porous graphene structure on a polyimide sheet. The formation 
and  structure  of  graphene  were  investigated  by  performing  microstructural  characterization  tests.  Silver 
nanoparticles  were  hybridized  into  the  graphene  structure  to  improve  the  sensor’s  performance  using  the 
sputtering  method.  Then,  the  electrodynamic  performance  of  the  sensor  without  additives  and  the  sensor 
containing  silver  nanoparticles  were  compared,  and  their  results  were  reported  in  tables  and  graphs.  The

Preparation of the laser-induced graphene (LIG)
Two  glass  slides  were  prepared  as  the  initial  substrate  for  LIG  (laser-induced  graphene)  and  Ag-coated  LIG 
samples. Kapton tape was attached to the slides using double-sided adhesive (Fig. 1a). The surface of the polyimide 
was cleaned with alcohol-soaked cotton to remove any contamination. Before graphene synthesis, optimizing 
the  parameters  of  the  samples  under  different  conditions  is  crucial.  The  laser  must  have  sufficient  power  to 
break the carbon bonds in the polyimide without damaging the graphene structure. Uniformity and graphene 
formation throughout the polyimide film require proper resolution adjustment. Laser writing was tested at levels 
ranging from 20% to 55%. Finally, the optimum power of 28% was selected as the most suitable power for both 
the bare and silver-coated samples to form graphene (Fig. 1b). Graphene synthesis was successfully performed 
on all three samples, and it was of good quality after adjusting the parameters of the laser system, including 
power, speed, resolution, and focal length. The samples were subjected to LIG treatment using a GCC LaserPro 
C180 II machine capable of producing laser irradiation with a power of 40 W.

Characterization  tests,  including  Raman  spectroscopy,  SEM,  EDS,  FESEM,  and  TEM  imaging,  were 
performed to quantitatively and qualitatively investigate the structure of LIG and to interpret the distribution of 
silver nanoparticles within the nanocomposite sensor.

4

Sputter coating of silver and preparation of PDMS nanocomposite film
Silver was deposited on the Kapton substrate after the laser-induced graphene (LIG) process, ensuring effective 
integration of the silver nanoparticles with the laser-induced graphene (Fig. 1c). To achieve this, the sample was 
placed in a Desk Sputter Coater DSR1 vacuum deposition system and coated with silver for 300 seconds. The 
coating process was controlled solely by the sputtering duration. Since the coating thickness was not directly 
essential, the coating time was adjusted by measuring the sheet conductance of the silver-coated LIG samples. 
After  300  seconds  of  sputtering,  the  sheet  conductance  did  not  change,  indicating  complete  coverage  and 
adequacy of the coating process. This is discussed in detail in33–35.

After sputtering, Sylgard 184 PDMS polymer from Dow Corning was used to create a polymer substrate with 
the desired mechanical properties. For this purpose, the PDMS resin was combined with the crosslinker at a 1:10 
ratio by hand for 10 minutes. To remove bubbles, the mixture was placed in a desiccator connected to a vacuum 
pump to remove all trapped air. A plexiglass mold, not shown in the figure to highlight other components, was 
attached to the glass with double-sided tape to enclose each sample completely (Fig. 1d). These molds, designed 
with precise dimensions and sealed completely, must be used to ensure the uniformity of the polymer thickness 
throughout the mold and the maintenance of the composite film’s uniformity. Before pouring the polymer into 
the molds, the glass with the attached samples was placed on a perfectly level surface. The oven was also leveled 
before placing the samples inside. The samples were placed in the oven, and the location of the samples was 
leveled. The samples were then cured at 70°C for two hours (Fig. 1e). After curing and removing the samples 
from the oven, some time was allowed for the glass and mold to cool entirely before facilitating the separation 
process. Then, the mold was separated from the polymer with a surgical blade, and then the molds were gently 
removed from the glass with a spatula. Finally, the nanocomposite film was peeled off from the samples (Fig. 1f) 
to provide the final nanocomposite sensor (Fig. 1g).

Each synthesized sensor element was cut to standard dimensions, and the resulting linear strain behavior 
was evaluated using tensile testing (5 cm in length and 5 mm in width). The strain sensing performance of strain 
sensors can be fully characterized by factors including stretchability, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, response 
and recovery time, and dynamic durability. Initially, the initial resistance of each element was measured by a 
multimeter and then placed in a tensile testing machine. Cyclic test parameters such as cyclic test type, number 
of cycles, applied strain level, and initial length were set in the appropriate software to use the desired tensile test 
for the samples.

Sensitivity
One of the most essential characteristics of a strain sensor element is its sensitivity to input excitation. Sensitivity 
is primarily dependent on the material structure (sensor materials) and secondarily on its geometry (sensor film 
thickness and its geometric pattern). The sensitivity of the sensor element is evaluated by a parameter called the 
gauge factor, or GF for short . According to the definition, the gauge factor is the response of the relative change 
in electrical resistance to mechanical strain and is calculated using the following equation36,37:

GF =

(1)

In this equation, R represents the electrical resistance after deformation, R0 represents the initial resistance, L 
and L0 represent the initial and post-deformation geometrical sizes, and ε denotes the strain. Typically, metallic 
strain gauges have an initial resistance of 120 or 350 Ω and a gauge factor of 2 to 5 (2 < GF < 5). This means that 
∆R in metallic strain gauges is very low (0.00024 Ω < ∆R < 0.24 Ω) because the flexibility and elasticity of their 
metal foils are very limited. Therefore, this category of strain gauges is only suitable for measuring microstrains 
(10−6 < ε < 10−3) and is of no help in measuring strains present in large deformations. This is where the need 
for new materials for advanced applications such as electronic skins arises, which are both highly sensitive and 
capable of monitoring large strains.

meta.title: Silver-decorated laser-induced graphene for a linear, sensitive, and almost hysteresis-free piezoresistive strain sensor.

raw:
www.nature.com/scientificreports

Silver-decorated laser-induced 
graphene for a linear, sensitive, 
and almost hysteresis-free 
piezoresistive strain sensor

Fatemehsadat Abedheydari1, Sadegh Sadeghzadeh1, Mohammad Saadatbakhsh1,2, 
Amirhossein Heydariyan1 & Elnaz Khakpour1

A new approach has recently emerged in graphene synthesis by direct laser writing (LIG), which is 
highly economical and scalable, unlike previous methods. Here, the sputtering method has been used 
to coat silver onto the laser-induced graphene-based sensor. The results demonstrate that the chosen 
approach substantially impacts the expected outcomes. The initial resistance values were consistent 
across the different sensor samples. The average resistance was slightly lower in the silver-coated 
samples compared to the uncoated samples, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Ag coating in 
enhancing the electrical conductivity of the LIG material. However, the difference in resistance was not 
statistically significant. The electromechanical behavior of the Ag-coated LIG strain sensor was tested 
under cyclic tensile strain. The gauge factor increased from 12.9-14.7 for the uncoated LIG sensor to 
17.2-26.7 for the Ag-coated sensor, with the difference growing at higher strains. At 5%, 30%, and 
70% strain, the gauge factor increased by 30%, 80%, and 82%, respectively. Sensors measuring 1-70% 
strain were developed, enabling use in various applications. Blood pulse measurements showed 
the silver-coated sample produced more uniform and reliable results than the uncoated sample. 
The number of beats matched a commercial pulse oximeter. This sensitivity, linearity, and reliability 
demonstrate the potential for commercializing these sensors.

Keywords  Laser-induced graphene, Silver decorated, Graphene, Wearable electronic, Strain Sensor

In recent years, based on nanotechnology achievements, various flexible strain sensors have been developed that 
convert  mechanical  properties-dependent  variables  (such  as  stretching,  bending,  and  torsion)  into  electrical 
signals.  These  wearable  electronic  devices  can  monitor  human  health  status  in  real-time  and  accurately  by 
receiving  various  biological  or  physiological  stimuli.  Advanced  composite  materials  and  new  manufacturing 
processes have led to the production of unique devices tailored to specific healthcare applications (e.g., human 
motion detection1, heart rate2, blood pressure2, respiration3, sports activity monitoring4, smart textiles5, and soft 
robotics6). In addition, composite sensors are resistant to degradation due to the wide range of materials and 
innovative manufacturing methods. Unlike conventional sensors, they have a particular tensile behavior and 
sensitivity.

However, given the widespread use of these sensors, several essential requirements and considerations must 
be considered. To better monitor signal complexity, the strain sensor must be sufficiently flexible and highly 
sensitive, have a wide measurement range, be fast-response capable, have excellent durability, and be compact.

Traditional  commercial  wearables,  mainly  in  the  form  of  glasses,  watches,  wristbands,  or  belts,  are  made 
entirely or partially of flat, stiff materials that require rigid supports or additional flexible straps to be attached 
to the human body. Therefore, clinical devices that use existing wearables can cause discomfort and limit the 
laboratory’s  monitoring  of  human  physiological  data.  This  significant  limitation  must  be  overcome  despite 
the growing market for wearables in broader screening outside the lab. Therefore, bulky and stiff plastics and 
metal  parts  in  sensors  and  electronics  must  be  replaced  with  skin-like  materials  to  increase  wearability  and 
performance. Specifically, such electronics provide stable and compliant contact with soft human skin without 
adding additional mechanical or thermal loads or causing skin breakdown. Current development approaches 
for advanced wearable, flexible hybrid electronics (WFHE) focus on soft and flexible form factors, non-irritating

of Science and Technology, Tehran, Iran. 2Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Kharazmi 
University, Tehran, Iran. email: sadeghzadeh@iust.ac.ir

Scientific Reports |        (2024) 14:28715 

| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-80158-y

1

OPEN www.nature.com/scientificreports/

and non-toxic properties, fully autonomous energy components, integrated wireless communications, and cost-
effective processes7. It should be noted that these complex features must be designed to meet the demanding 
requirements of advanced physiological recording from the human body.

Conductive polymer composites (CPCs) have been used as strain-sensing materials due to their advantages 
of being lightweight, low cost, good processability, high sensitivity, and environmental compatibility7. They have 
created  new  opportunities  for  fabricating  high-performance  strain-sensing  devices  cost-effectively.  In  CPC-
based  strain  sensors,  the  change  in  conductive  networks  under  applied  strain  produces  an  output  electrical 
signal,  enabling  them  to  detect  external  stress  stimuli.  To  improve  the  properties  mentioned  above,  various 
strategies are employed in the fabrication of CPC strain sensors:

•  Modulating the ratios of conductive fillers
•  Incorporating hybrid fillers into a polymer matrix
•  Functionalizing the surface of conductive fillers
•  Tailoring the orientation and distribution of conductive fillers

Composite sensors have two main parts: 1) a polymer matrix and 2) a conductive filler. The conductive fillers 
create a continuous conductive path in the polymer matrix, which is responsible for the electrical and mechanical 
properties of the sensor that transfer mechanical stimuli to the conductive network.

In this context, piezoresistive sensors with a mechanism for converting applied strain into electrical resistance 
have been used in applications to monitor structural changes. One of the popular polymers in this field used 
as the substrate for these sensors is a thermoset polymer called polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)8. It has unique 
properties such as transparency, non-fluorescence, non-toxicity, biocompatibility, stable thermal and chemical 
properties, unique physical properties, and high flexibility. PDMS has no adhesion to polymer layers, an essential 
advantage for its application in MEMS and biomedical technology9.

Graphene  is  a  promising  material  for  fillers  due  to  its  exceptional  properties,  such  as  high  electrical 
conductivity and desirable mechanical strength10. Researchers have reported producing porous graphene using 
laser irradiation, namely laser-induced graphene (LIG). The ability to rapidly synthesize graphene foam using 
the LIG method has revolutionized the fabrication and production of sensors incorporating graphene as a filler 
material. This method has advantages such as being simple, low-cost, and suitable for producing graphene over 
a  large  area11.  This  method  produces  LIG  patterns  in  a  non-contact  process  via  direct  laser  engraving  on  a 
polyimide (PI) film. In terms of piezoresistive performance, the changes in the pore size of the LIG foam, the 
electrical contact between its walls, and the quantum tunneling phenomenon create significant sensitivity in the 
sensor.

Hybrid nanomaterials
Nanomaterials with different dimensions, such as silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), silver nanowires, gold nanowires, 
graphene, carbon black, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs), can be combined with graphene using various deposition 
methods12–18. This approach helps maintain high conductivity under various strains and excellent stability.

Graphene is a two-dimensional structure consisting of a single layer of the carbon honeycomb lattice. Due 
to its exceptional electrical conductivity, carrier mobility, and mechanical properties, graphene has become a 
unique material. This new solid-state system is a suitable substitute for the next generation of advanced micro 
and  nanoelectromechanical  devices.  Therefore,  it  has  attracted  unprecedented  attention  in  fundamental  and 
applied research.

Graphene  can  be  produced  using  methods  such  as  mechanical  exfoliation  of  graphite,  chemical  vapor 
deposition  on  metals  from  hydrocarbon  gas  precursors,  thermal  decomposition,  and  reduction  of  graphene 
oxide. Laser irradiation of a polymer precursor to induce photochemical and thermal conversion to graphene is 
another method for producing graphene. Graphene obtained in this way is usually called laser-induced graphene 
(LIG) or laser graphene (LSG). LIG has a slightly lower quality than graphene obtained by other methods, but 
relative simplicity and low cost are the main advantages of laser induction.

The surface morphology of LIG is characterized by a complex and inhomogeneous porous pattern resulting 
from the rapid production of gases during irradiation and the sp3→ sp2 carbon conversion, an example of a 
flat graphene structure. The inhomogeneous structure is also due to defects in the regular arrangement of C 
atoms,  as  5-  or  7-membered  carbon  rings  can  be  found  that  slightly  bend  the  regular  hexagonal  network19. 
LIG’s  composition  and  morphology  and  its  electrical,  mechanical,  and  surface  properties  depend  on  factors 
such as the type of laser and the processing parameters. With precise control of laser parameters during the laser 
scribing process, graphene is obtained in porous and nanofiber-organized structures. LIG generally has high 
graphene conductivity, large specific surface area, strain, and corrosion resistance and can also be functionalized 
to catalyze reactions or sense strain, temperature, magnetic field intensity, and chemical concentration20.

Unlike  traditional  synthesis  routes  based  on  the  thermal  decomposition  of  resins  at  high  temperatures 
(around 1200 °C) in an inert atmosphere, the laser line enables the fabrication of porous carbon structures by 
performing in situ synthesis on a polymer substrate and patterning in the form of fully customizable electrodes 
and circuits.

Polyimide (PI) films
Polyimide (PI) films are readily available in sheets, rolls, and even tapes with a wide range of thicknesses and are 
the first and most popular precursor substrates for LIG production. PI is also widely used to produce flexible 
electronics due to its high strength and chemical and thermal stability. The chemical structure of PI appears to 
be particularly suitable for LIG production, as 2sp aromatic carbons are more prone to form hexagonal graphene 
structures than other precursors that only produce amorphous carbon.

Laser irradiation of PI
Irradiation of polyimide with UV laser pulses, when the laser fluence is 100–500mJ/cm2, causes local heating at 
the target spot and increases the surface temperature to 1700 °C. These results are further supported by molecular 
dynamics (MD) simulations, which show that the conversion to LIG occurs at high pressure and temperature. 
The energy available is sufficient to break down C-N, C-O, C-H, and C-O19,21–23.

The  D3  structure  is  more  sensitive  to  similar  strain  than  the  flat  structure.  Similarly,  the  sensor  can  be 
designed  with  a  corrugated  structure  to  improve  sensitivity. The  corrugated  structure  allows  the  stress  to  be 
concentrated on the indentations when the sensor is stretched, and the resistance will change significantly24.

Sensor composition
Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a thermoset polymer, is the most/one the most commonly used sensor substrate 
due to its unique properties, including transparency, non-fluorescence, non-toxicity, biocompatibility, stability 
in thermal and chemical conditions, unique physical properties, and flexibility.

This polymer is a neutral, non-toxic, and non-flammable silicone elastomer with a leading O-Si chain and a 
repeating Si(CH3)2O unit. Its molecular weight generally varies from 10 to 60 thousand grams per mole, and its 
specific gravity ranges from 0.91 to 1.0025–27.

PDMS has a mineral backbone with organic groups as pendants, classified as a "semi-mineral" or "organo-
mineral" polymer. PDMS and silica composites have relatively high impact strength, determining a material’s 
ability to resist sudden fracture force. Using standard impact tests, such as the Charpy pendulum and drop weight 
impact  tests  on  PDMS  composites,  it  has  been  concluded  that  the  impact  strength  increases  with  increasing 
PDMS  content  in  a  composite28.  It  behaves  like  an  elastomer  because  the  glass  transition  temperature  of  its 
siloxane component is much lower than at room temperature. As a result, it can absorb large amounts of energy 
during impact testing and delay crack and fracture formation28,29.

The  graphene-based  composite  has  excellent  electrical  properties  because  the  contacts  between  platinum 
nanoparticles and the graphene network create many conductive tunnels. Notably, the experimental results show 
high sensitivity (GFmax = 489.3) and a broad strain range of up to 20% of the platinum/graphene composite 
matrix after deposition on a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrate, which shows a significant performance 
compared to the LIG strain sensor on a polyimide substrate without platinum nanoparticles. Porous graphene 
with a large surface area can be formed by photochemical reactions and the photothermal effect introduced by 
ultraviolet laser. The surface of graphene flakes is rough with granular textures, resulting from the rapid pulsed 
laser process. The TEM image shows that the nano-sized platinum particles are homogeneously distributed on 
the graphene sheet30. It initially increases with increasing platinum loading and then decreases with increasing 
platinum content to 2.0 mmol. The gauge factor was 45.6 at (0–6%), 269.5 at (6–16%), and 489.3 at (16–20%) 
at a platinum concentration of 1.0 mmol. It is also worth noting that the hysteresis in the device was primarily 
suppressed with the addition of 1.0 mmol of platinum30.

The rational combination with highly conductive graphene may limit the electrical conductivity of the 2MoS-
LIG  nanocomposite.  Still,  the  intrinsic  active  hierarchical  structure  of  2Mos  and  the  synergistic  interaction 
between the composite layers reduce the fracture of graphene nanosheets to certain strain limits31. Laser scribing 
of a few-layered 2Mos coated on commercial PI film using a CO2 infrared laser creates 3D porous graphene 
decorated with MoS2, which enables superior electromechanical properties. The high-sensitivity sensor response 
(GF = 1242), low hysteresis, ultra-low detection limit, wide working range, and long-term reliability (over 12000 
cycles) were demonstrated.

Considering  the  advantages  of  the  LIG  method  in  sensor  manufacturing,  such  as  scalability  and  cost-
effectiveness, although the graphene obtained by this method has a similar quality to other laboratory methods 
with a slight decrease in electrical properties, with techniques such as hybridization with secondary nano-fillers, 
creating micro-cracks and manipulating the sensor geometry, a significant increase in the basic properties of 
the sensor can be made. The primary novelty of the current approach lies in the application of silver decoration 
via sputtering to enhance the performance of laser-induced graphene (LIG) strain sensors. This is crucial for 
accurate measurements in various applications, as it allows the sensor to detect even small changes in strain 
with high precision. Moreover, the silver decoration enhances the stability of the sensor under cyclic loading 
conditions, addressing common challenges faced by other graphene-based sensors. This improved stability and 
reliability are essential for the long-term performance and durability of the sensor in real-world applications. 
Here,  the  sputtering  method  has  been  used  to  coat  silver  onto  the  laser-induced  graphene-based  sensor. 
Considering sputtering’s capability at various penetration depths, this approach offers significant advantages, 
including  precise  control  and  high  design  flexibility.  Sputtering  was  studied  before  and  after  laser  treatment 
to investigate the effect of silver coating on the fabricated sensors, resulting in optimal conditions. The results 
demonstrate that the chosen approach substantially impacts the expected outcomes. Figure 1 depicts the steps 
for manufacturing the silver-coated strain sensors.

Preparation of the laser-induced graphene (LIG)
Two  glass  slides  were  prepared  as  the  initial  substrate  for  LIG  (laser-induced  graphene)  and  Ag-coated  LIG 
samples. Kapton tape was attached to the slides using double-sided adhesive (Fig. 1a). The surface of the polyimide 
was cleaned with alcohol-soaked cotton to remove any contamination. Before graphene synthesis, optimizing 
the  parameters  of  the  samples  under  different  conditions  is  crucial.  The  laser  must  have  sufficient  power  to 
break the carbon bonds in the polyimide without damaging the graphene structure. Uniformity and graphene 
formation throughout the polyimide film require proper resolution adjustment. Laser writing was tested at levels 
ranging from 20% to 55%. Finally, the optimum power of 28% was selected as the most suitable power for both 
the bare and silver-coated samples to form graphene (Fig. 1b). Graphene synthesis was successfully performed 
on all three samples, and it was of good quality after adjusting the parameters of the laser system, including 
power, speed, resolution, and focal length. The samples were subjected to LIG treatment using a GCC LaserPro 
C180 II machine capable of producing laser irradiation with a power of 40 W.

Characterization  tests,  including  Raman  spectroscopy,  SEM,  EDS,  FESEM,  and  TEM  imaging,  were 
performed to quantitatively and qualitatively investigate the structure of LIG and to interpret the distribution of 
silver nanoparticles within the nanocomposite sensor.

Sputter coating of silver and preparation of PDMS nanocomposite film
Silver was deposited on the Kapton substrate after the laser-induced graphene (LIG) process, ensuring effective 
integration of the silver nanoparticles with the laser-induced graphene (Fig. 1c). To achieve this, the sample was 
placed in a Desk Sputter Coater DSR1 vacuum deposition system and coated with silver for 300 seconds. The 
coating process was controlled solely by the sputtering duration. Since the coating thickness was not directly 
essential, the coating time was adjusted by measuring the sheet conductance of the silver-coated LIG samples. 
After  300  seconds  of  sputtering,  the  sheet  conductance  did  not  change,  indicating  complete  coverage  and 
adequacy of the coating process. This is discussed in detail in33–35.

After sputtering, Sylgard 184 PDMS polymer from Dow Corning was used to create a polymer substrate with 
the desired mechanical properties. For this purpose, the PDMS resin was combined with the crosslinker at a 1:10 
ratio by hand for 10 minutes. To remove bubbles, the mixture was placed in a desiccator connected to a vacuum 
pump to remove all trapped air. A plexiglass mold, not shown in the figure to highlight other components, was 
attached to the glass with double-sided tape to enclose each sample completely (Fig. 1d). These molds, designed 
with precise dimensions and sealed completely, must be used to ensure the uniformity of the polymer thickness 
throughout the mold and the maintenance of the composite film’s uniformity. Before pouring the polymer into 
the molds, the glass with the attached samples was placed on a perfectly level surface. The oven was also leveled 
before placing the samples inside. The samples were placed in the oven, and the location of the samples was 
leveled. The samples were then cured at 70°C for two hours (Fig. 1e). After curing and removing the samples 
from the oven, some time was allowed for the glass and mold to cool entirely before facilitating the separation 
process. Then, the mold was separated from the polymer with a surgical blade, and then the molds were gently 
removed from the glass with a spatula. Finally, the nanocomposite film was peeled off from the samples (Fig. 1f) 
to provide the final nanocomposite sensor (Fig. 1g).

Each synthesized sensor element was cut to standard dimensions, and the resulting linear strain behavior 
was evaluated using tensile testing (5 cm in length and 5 mm in width). The strain sensing performance of strain 
sensors can be fully characterized by factors including stretchability, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, response 
and recovery time, and dynamic durability. Initially, the initial resistance of each element was measured by a 
multimeter and then placed in a tensile testing machine. Cyclic test parameters such as cyclic test type, number 
of cycles, applied strain level, and initial length were set in the appropriate software to use the desired tensile test 
for the samples.

Sensitivity
One of the most essential characteristics of a strain sensor element is its sensitivity to input excitation. Sensitivity 
is primarily dependent on the material structure (sensor materials) and secondarily on its geometry (sensor film 
thickness and its geometric pattern). The sensitivity of the sensor element is evaluated by a parameter called the 
gauge factor, or GF for short . According to the definition, the gauge factor is the response of the relative change 
in electrical resistance to mechanical strain and is calculated using the following equation36,37:

In this equation, R represents the electrical resistance after deformation, R0 represents the initial resistance, L 
and L0 represent the initial and post-deformation geometrical sizes, and ε denotes the strain. Typically, metallic 
strain gauges have an initial resistance of 120 or 350 Ω and a gauge factor of 2 to 5 (2 < GF < 5). This means that 
∆R in metallic strain gauges is very low (0.00024 Ω < ∆R < 0.24 Ω) because the flexibility and elasticity of their 
metal foils are very limited. Therefore, this category of strain gauges is only suitable for measuring microstrains 
(10−6 < ε < 10−3) and is of no help in measuring strains present in large deformations. This is where the need 
for new materials for advanced applications such as electronic skins arises, which are both highly sensitive and 
capable of monitoring large strains.

The previous section described the fabrication process of the nanosensors, and all the optimized parameters, 
from laser power to data control and processing, were presented to ensure successful graphene synthesis. This

According to the Raman spectroscopy results (Fig. 2), peaks corresponding to graphene were observed. The G

the layer thickness. The intensity of the G band can be used to assess the thickness of graphene.

EDS test results
This  test  examines  the  percentage  of  oxygen  and  carbon  elements  in  the  LIG  microstructure.  Carbon-rich 
areas are shown in red, and oxygen-rich areas in green. According to Fig. 4, the red areas are more dominant, 
indicating that the structure is mainly composed of carbon, which is a sign of the presence of graphene. The 
dark red color probably means that multilayer graphene hierarchical structures are repeated one after another. 
The green areas emphasize the presence of graphene oxide (GO) in the structure. The image shows that oxygen 
is more concentrated at the boundaries of graphene layers and pores. This can be explained by the fact that in 
these areas, due to the presence of incomplete bonds of carbon atoms at the boundaries, which are caused by 
the lack of enough neighboring carbon atoms to saturate the carbon atom capacity, oxygen atoms have enough 
opportunity to bond with carbon atoms, resulting in the production of oxides in the structure.

The structure obtained from higher powers has a redder color (laser power of 28%, Fig. 4b-right) than the areas 
lasered with lower power (laser power of 25%, Fig. 4b-left). This can be attributed to the higher graphitization 
degree and higher accumulation of graphene layers due to higher temperatures. Since the porosities are smaller, 
the boundary regions are also reduced, and less oxygen can oxidize the structure. The higher ratio of carbon atoms 
to oxygen at higher power is also numerically confirmed in the EDS test. As can be seen from the elemental ratio 
diagram, the carbon-to-oxygen ratios for powers (25%) and (28%) were obtained as 87.51:12.49 and 92.32:7.68, 
respectively, indicating the ability to synthesize purer graphene at higher laser power.

The gauge factor (GF), a critical parameter for quantifying the piezoresistive sensitivity of the sensors, was 
analyzed as a function of the applied compressive strain, as shown in Fig. 10. The gauge factor was in the range 
of 13.5 to 14.7 for the uncoated LIG sensor. Specifically, the GF remained relatively constant at around 13.5 for 
the strain range of 5% to 30%. However, at the highest tested strain level of 70%, the GF increased slightly to 
14.7. In contrast, incorporating the silver (Ag) coating led to a significant enhancement in the piezoresistive 
sensitivity of the sensor. The GF range for the Ag-coated LIG sensor spanned from 17.7 at 5% strain to 26.7 at 
70%  strain.  Notably,  adding  the  Ag  coating  did  not  substantially  change  the  sensor’s  initial  resistance. These 
findings  demonstrate  that  the  Ag-coated  LIG  sensor  notably  improves  piezoresistive  sensitivity  compared  to 
the uncoated LIG sensor, as evidenced by the higher gauge factor values across the entire strain range tested. 
Importantly, this enhancement in GF was achieved without significantly altering the baseline electrical properties 
of the uncoated LIG material. Figure 10 shows a steep increase in the gauge factor for the Ag-Coated LIG sensor 
between 5% and 10% strain. The observed steep increase in GF within this strain range can be attributed to 
several factors. Initially, at lower strains (up to 5%), the sensor primarily experiences elastic deformation, where 
the piezoresistive response is relatively linear and modest. However, as the strain increases from 5% to 10%, 
the  material  undergoes  significant  microstructural  changes,  including  the  alignment  of  graphene  layers  and 
the redistribution of charge carriers. These changes enhance electron mobility and lead to a more pronounced 
piezoresistive effect, resulting in the steep increase in GF observed in this range. Interestingly, this steep change 
is primarily confined to the 5% to 10% strain interval. Beyond 10% strain, the gauge factor continues to increase 
but at a much slower rate. The saturation of the piezoresistive response can explain this behavior. As the strain 
increases further, the material may reach a point where the response becomes more stable and less sensitive 
to additional strain, leading to a gradual change in GF rather than a steep increase. The interaction between 
the  silver  coating  and  the  LIG  matrix  may  also  influence  the  gauge  factor.  Silver  nanoparticles  enhance  the 
piezoresistive response, but this effect may stabilize as the strain increases, contributing to the observed behavior.

and laser scribing offer more straightforward and cost-effective fabrication processes. These methods may be 
preferable for applications where cost and ease of production are critical factors despite potentially lower gauge 
factors. Our Ag-Coated LIG sensor, fabricated by direct laser writing followed by silver sputtering, exhibits a 
gauge factor ranging from 17.7 to 26.7 over a strain range of 5% to 70%. This performance is comparable to or 
exceeds that of some other sensors while being inferior to that of others, such as the graphene sensor fabricated by 
direct laser writing alone (GF of 20 at 20% strain) and the carbon nanotube (CNT) sensor manufactured by CVD 
and Ecoflex (GF of 1.25–9.25 at 5–400% strain). The materials employed in these sensors also vary significantly. 
For  example,  reduced  graphene  oxide  (RGO)  drop  casting  combined  with  silver  nanoparticles  demonstrates 
a  high  gauge  factor  475.  Each  sensor  has  its  fabrication  costs  and  specifications,  influencing  its  commercial 
viability.  For  instance,  while  the  nanographene  sensor  offers  high  sensitivity,  its  complex  fabrication  process 
may limit its widespread use compared to more straightforward methods that yield adequate performance at 
a  lower  cost.  Our  experience  with  laser-induced  graphene  (LIG)  sensors  has  shown  that  their  specifications 
depend highly on the laser machine used and the parameters set during fabrication. Laser power, speed, and 
environment variations can lead to differences in gauge factor and strain response, which may not be directly 
comparable to sensors fabricated using different methods or materials.

As illustrated in Fig. 11a,b, the resistance change versus applied strain plots for the LIG and Ag-coated LIG 
sensor configurations demonstrated high linearity. The experimental data points aligned closely with linear trend 
lines, indicating that the sensors exhibit a linear piezoresistive response over the measured strain ranges. While 
not perfectly linear, the resistance change behavior can be approximated as linear with high accuracy. This linear

| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-80158-y

14

 
 
 www.nature.com/scientificreports/

relationship  between  resistance  change  and  strain  is  a  desirable  characteristic  that  facilitates  straightforward 
interpretation and modeling of the sensor output. The linearity of the sensor response is a critical performance 
metric, as it enables predictable and reliable operation in various sensing applications.

To ensure the fabricated sensors’ stability and linear behavior, the sensor’s relative resistance changes during 
the strain loading-unloading cycles are plotted versus time over 50 cycles in Fig. 12. Figure 12 shows the linear 
response  of  the  uncoated  sensor  element  to  50  identical  loading-unloading  cycles  under  20%  strain.  As  can 
be seen, the sensor resistance is maximum in the first cycle and gradually decreases during the first ten cycles 
when it is subjected to strain. After that, the resistance has a lower reduction and becomes almost constant after 
ten  cycles.  This  phenomenon  occurs  during  the  initial  ten  cycles  and  is  called  warm-up.  During  the  warm-
up phenomenon, the residual stress inside the polymer matrix is released due to stretching. When stretched, 
graphene nanosheets have the opportunity to rearrange themselves in a more parallel direction to each other to 
release this stress. This increases the order of the nanofillers, and their connection leads to an increase in electron 
conduction and, consequently, a decrease in resistance. After several cycles, this stress almost disappears, and the 
sensor resistance reaches a nearly constant value.

The  observed  differences  in  performance  between  the  Ag-coated  and  uncoated  LIG  sensors  can  be 
attributed to several physical mechanisms. The silver coating enhances the electrical conductivity of the LIG 
material, primarily due to the formation of conductive pathways provided by the silver nanoparticles. This is 
because the presence of metal nanoparticles can significantly improve the charge carrier mobility and reduce 
the  overall  resistance  of  graphene-based  materials.  In  this  study,  the  gauge  factor  of  the  Ag-coated  sensors 
increased significantly compared to the uncoated sensors, indicating a higher sensitivity to strain. This increase 
can be explained by the interaction between the silver nanoparticles and the LIG matrix, which enhances the 
piezoresistive effect. As strain is applied, the silver nanoparticles can redistribute and create additional conductive 
pathways, leading to a more pronounced change in resistance. Furthermore, the porous structure of the LIG 
allows for better adhesion and distribution of the silver nanoparticles, which contributes to the sensor’s overall 
stability and sensitivity. The increased LIG surface area and defect sites also facilitate better electron transfer, 
which is crucial for the piezoresistive response. In summary, the combination of enhanced conductivity from the 
silver coating, the structural characteristics of the LIG, and the interaction between the two materials contributes 
to the improved performance of the Ag-coated sensors.

Application: blood pulse measurement using fabricated sensors
One significant and exciting difference between the coated and uncoated sensor samples is the measurement 
of blood pulse, which produces deficient strains in the samples. Considering that the sensor must have high 
sensitivity for measuring pulse rate, a cyclic test with a maximum strain of 1% was conducted before using the 
sensor as a blood pulse measurement element. It is important to note that the equipment used for the cyclic

amplifies the sensor’s response to minor strains, enabling it to detect minute changes in pressure corresponding 
to blood pulses. The sensors are designed to operate effectively within a dynamic range of strains from 5% to 
70%; however, their linearity and reliability facilitate accurate measurement of lower strains, allowing them to 
capture the dynamics of blood pressure pulses despite their small magnitude.

of the Ag coating in enhancing the electrical conductivity of the LIG material. However, it is essential to note

the addition of conductive nano-fillers is performed to increase the gauge factor in different strain ranges, the 
electromechanical behavior of the Ag-coated LIG strain sensor was tested under cyclic tensile strain at strains

24.2, 24.5, and 26.7, respectively. This sensitivity increase is due to the presence of silver nanoparticles and the 
subsequent  creation  of  more  conductive  paths,  which  occurs  with  quantum  tunneling  compared  with  gauge 
factors of 12.9, 13.5, 13.7, 13.6, 13.5, 13.6, and 14.7 for uncoated LIG sensors. As expected, with increasing strain, 
the sensor resistance increases, and consequently, the relative resistance changes also increase. Similar to what 
was observed for the reference sensor, the gradual decrease in the residual effect was also observed in the Ag-
coated LIG sensor with increasing strain percentage. The sensor showed no signs of performance degradation 
up to 100%. However, the sensor had a tensile limit in both cases without a secondary filler and containing silver 
nanoparticles, and stretching more than the mentioned strain caused the sensor to break.

The linear behavior of the sensor containing silver nanoparticles (Ag-coated LIG) is, on average, 15–20% 
lower than that of the sensor with pure graphene (LIG) in the structure. This can be attributed to weak bonds 
and poor adhesion between silver nanoparticles and the polymer matrix, which leads to the displacement of 
conductive pathways during stretching cycles.

Adding silver increases the gauge factor of the sensor. By comparing the graphs at different strains, it can 
be concluded that with increasing strain in the range of (5%−70%), the difference in gauge factor between the 
uncoated LIG and Ag-coated LIG sensors increases. At 5%, 30%, and 70% strain, the gauge factor increases by 
30%, 80%, and 82%, respectively.

In  general,  although  the  conductive  nanoparticles  increased  the  piezoresistive  sensitivity  by  a  maximum 
of 82%, the linearity behavior of the hybridized sample changed for higher strains. This behavior is due to the 
higher degree of freedom and the inevitable mobility of silver nanoparticles in the polymer matrix. On the other 
hand, the LIG sensor has linear stability with almost no significant change in all applied strain ranges.

Sensors capable of measuring minimum and maximum strains of 5% and 70% have been developed, enabling

title: Hydrogels and nanogels: effectiveness in dermal applications.

sections.text:
Methods involving polymer mixtures generate thermo-sensitive
hydrogels,  such  as  chitosan/β-glycerophosphate/collagen-
based  hydrogels  [129].  In  another  example,  hydrogels
comprised of gelatin microspheres, glutaraldehyde – as a cross-
linker, added to Pluronic F127 and F68 can vary from sol to gel
phases by changing both temperature and polymer concentra-
tion [130].

Chitosan-based hydrogels have aroused a lot of interest in the
health sciences field due to their biocompatibility, biodegrad-
ability, and low cytotoxicity [131]. This makes them attractive
as a promising material for topical administration of biomole-
cules such as nucleic acids and proteins [48,132].

Different techniques have been tested for the preparation of
chitosan hydrogels, including ionotropic gelation [76], emul-
sion  polymerization [108],  and  copolymerization [57,133].
Chitosan can be cross-linked with several organic and inorgan-
ic compounds due to its amine (NH2) and hydroxyl (OH) func-
tional groups [77], as shown in Figure 1. The stability of hydro-
gels  is  maintained  by  cross-links  that,  in  aqueous  media,
prevent  the  dissolution  of  polymer  chains  [134].

Another polymer widely used in the preparation of hydrogels is
cellulose. Cellulose hydrogels have become attractive due to
their  high  biocompatibility  and  long  circulating  time  in  the
blood, as well as low cytotoxicity [73]. They can be prepared
by various methods, including phase inversion [73], copolymer-
ization [110,111], and double chemical cross-linking reaction
[51].

Cellulose derivatives, such as cellulose ether [90], carboxy-
methyl cellulose (CMC) [82], hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC)
[113], or cellulose nanofibers [135] yield valuable hydrogels.

Keratin hydrogels are interesting for the properties of keratin, as
they have intrinsic biocompatibility, therapeutic activity, and
favorable physical properties [136]. They can be formed by pre-
paring an aqueous solution of keratin at concentrations of 8 or
20%, for example [137]. With the "disulfide shuffling" method,
phosphate-buffered  saline  (PBS)  is  used  to  dissolve  15%
lyophilized keratin and 1.5% cysteine. This solution requires
vigorous stirring followed by rest to form the gel [138]. Keratin
concentrations varied between 10, 15, and 20% in water, and
vigorous  agitation  was  used  for  dissolution [136].  Then,  to
promote the formation of disulfide bonds, a 5% solution of
H2O2 is added. For gel formation, mixtures should be incubat-
ed overnight at 37 °C.

Collagen-based hydrogels can be developed by using different
sources of collagen. Both plant and animal protein sources can
provide raw materials needed for adequate collagen production,
which includes rat tail tendons [84,86,139], goat tendons [87],
swine skin [88], and gelatin [87]. The collagen concentration
may vary in the resulting hydrogels (e.g., from 1.5% [84] to
30% [85]).

Polyvinyl alcohol hydrogels can be obtained in several ways,
which include dissolving PVA in water at 90 °C with the addi-
tion of PEG-200, followed by freezing and thawing cycles. For
the formation of hydrogel films, drying for four days at room
temperature and storage in a desiccator is required [94]. In the
method described by Gao et al. (2018), PVA 15% w/v is added
into water and stirred at 95 °C until complete dissolution [55].
The freeze/thaw cycle was carried out at −20 °C and room tem-
perature and by electronic beam irradiation.

Polyvinyl alcohol hydrogels can be used for wound healing.
Suhaeri et al. (2018) manufactured an adhesive hydrogel with
PVA and a derivative of human pulmonary fibroblasts, in addi-
tion to ciprofloxacin, for treating infected wounds [95]. For the
preparation of the human pulmonary fibroblast derivative, the
cells were cultured for seven days in a modified Eagle’s medi-
um and then decellularized by washing several times with PBS.
Then a 7% aqueous PVA solution was added to the pulmonary
fibroblast derivative. For the cross-linking of the solution, the
freeze/thaw method was performed, followed by ultrasound for

water at 90 °C, with separate addition of sodium alginate and
glucomannan polysaccharide [140]. The freeze/thaw process
was repeated three times. The cross-linking was done with satu-
rated  solutions  of  Ca(OH)2  (pH  10.2),  CaCl2  (pH  7.2),  or
